1033: \subsection{Parton distribution function uncertainties}
1034: \label{sec:pdfu}
1035: 
1036: Because we are interested in heavy particles, the parton distribution
1037: functions (PDFs) will be probed at large values of the proton's
1038: momentum fraction.  Hence, as opposed to Drell-Yan or $s$-channel
1039: single-top-quark production where the PDFs are well understood, we
1040: expect the PDF uncertainty to play a significant role in the total
1041: uncertainty of the cross section.  In order to estimate the effects of
1042: this uncertainty we use a modification
1043: \cite{Sullivan:2001ry,Nadolsky:2001yg} of the ``tolerance method''
1044: implemented in the CTEQ6 PDFs \cite{Pumplin:2002vw}.
1045: 
1046: The tolerance method is based on diagonalization of the matrix of
1047: second derivatives for $\chi^{2}$ (a Hessian matrix) near the minimum
1048: of $\chi^{2}$ for the PDF fits \cite{Pumplin:2001ct}.  Since
1049: $\chi^{2}$ is approximately parabolic near its minimum $\chi^{2}_{0}$,
1050: hypersurfaces of constant $\chi^{2}$ are hyperellipses in the space of
1051: the original 20 PDF parameters $\{a_{i}\}$.  These hyperellipses are
1052: transformed into hyperspheres by a change of coordinates
1053: $\{a_{i}\}\rightarrow \{z_{i}\},\, i=1,\dots ,20$.  The tolerance
1054: method assumes that all acceptable PDF sets correspond to a $\chi^{2}$
1055: that does not exceed their minimal value $\chi _{0}^{2}$ more than by
1056: $T^{2}$.  As a result, the acceptable PDF sets have $\{z_{i}\}$ within
1057: a sphere of the radius $T^{2}$ around $\{z_{i}(\chi _{0}^{2})\}\equiv
1058: \{z_{i}^{0}\}$.  In principle, $T$ should be chosen to correspond to a
1059: $1\sigma$ deviation of the fit.  However, for simplicity we present
1060: results for $T=10$, as used by the CTEQ6M101 -- CTEQ6M140 PDF tables
1061: given in Ref. \cite{Pumplin:2002vw}.
1062: 
1063: The PDF uncertainty for an observable $O$ is the maximal change in $O$
1064: as a function of variables $\{z_{i}\}$ varying within the tolerance
1065: hypersphere.  The CTEQ6 paper estimates the variation of $O$ by using
1066: a master formula
1067: \begin{equation}
1068: \label{eq:tolmast}
1069: \delta O=\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\sum^{20}_{i=1}\delta O_{i}^{2}},\mbox {\,
1070: where\, }\delta O_{i}\equiv T\frac{\partial O}{\partial z_{i}}\approx
1071: T\frac{O(z^{0}_{i}+t)-O(z^{0}_{i}-t)}{t} \;,
1072: \end{equation}
1073: and $t=10$ is a step in the space of $z_{i}$.  Here, $O(z_{1}^{0},\dots
1074: ,z_{i}^{0}\pm t,\dots ,z_{20}^{0})$ is denoted as $O(z_{i}^{0}\pm t)$.
1075: Eq.~(\ref{eq:tolmast}) is a good approximation for the PDF fits, but is
1076: less useful for observables, e.g.\ cross sections.
1077: 
1078: The difficulty with Eq.~(\ref{eq:tolmast}) is well exemplified for the
1079: problem at hand by Fig.~\ref{fig:errasm}.  Here we see the uncertainty
1080: for each of the 20 pairs of PDFs as a function of the parameters $z_i$
1081: for $m_{\wprm} = 500$ GeV.  If we apply Eq.~(\ref{eq:tolmast}) we would
1082: predict an uncertainty of $\pm 5.9\%$.  However,
1083: $O(z^{0}_{i}+t)-O(z^{0}_{i}-t) \approx 0$ for nearly half of the
1084: parameters, even though Fig.~\ref{fig:errasm} shows that these provide
1085: a large deviation.  The uncertainty in Eq.~(\ref{eq:tolmast}) appears to
1086: be more sensitive to $z_i$ which have a small absolute effect, but
1087: happen to cause a shift in the prediction which changes sign, than to
1088: large fluctuations.  This defect of the master formula is a result of
1089: the simple observation that the PDF set that minimizes the uncertainty
1090: in a given observable $O$ is not necessarily the same as the one that
1091: minimizes the fit to the global data set.
1092: 
1093: \begin{figure}[tbh]
1094: \epsfxsize=3.4in
1095: \centerline{\epsfbox{tpdferr.ps}} 
1096: \caption{Uncertainty in the cross section for $m_{\wprm} = 500$ GeV
1097: for each pair of PDFs using CTEQ6M1xx.  Circles are odd PDF sets.
1098: Squares are even PDF sets.\label{fig:errasm}}
1099: \end{figure}
1100: 
1101: In order to obtain a better estimator of the uncertainty of a generic
1102: observable $O$, we introduce \cite{Sullivan:2001ry,Nadolsky:2001yg} the
1103: ``modified tolerance method'' (MTM) master formula.  We define the maximum
1104: positive and negative errors on an observable $O$ by
1105: \begin{eqnarray}
1106: \delta O_{+} & = & \frac{T}{t}\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{20}\Bigl( \max 
1107: [\,O(z^{0}_{i}+t)-O(z_{i}^{0}),O(z^{0}_{i}-t)-O(z_{i}^{0}),0]\Bigr)^2}
1108: \;,\label{eq:pdferra} \\
1109: \delta O_{-} & = & \frac{T}{t}\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{20}\Bigl( \max 
1110: [\,O(z_{i}^{0})-O(z^{0}_{i}+t),O(z_{i}^{0})-O(z^{0}_{i}-t),0]\Bigr)^2}
1111: \; ,\label{eq:pdferr}
1112: \end{eqnarray}
1113: where the ``tolerance'' $T$ is the same scaling parameter that
1114: determines the overall range of allowed variation of $\chi^2$, and we
1115: use $T=t=10$ as in the CTEQ6 PDF sets.  In
1116: Eqs.~(\ref{eq:pdferra}, \ref{eq:pdferr}) we sum the maximum deviations
1117: on the observable in each of the parameter directions, and hence
1118: retain both maximal sensitivity to the parameters that vary the most
1119: and estimate the range of allowed values of the cross section.  Given
1120: the case in Fig.~\ref{fig:errasm}, we determine that $m_{\wprm} = 500$
1121: GeV has an uncertainty of ${+8.6}{-6.2}\%$ --- half again as large
1122: on the high side as estimated by the CTEQ method.

1124: \subsection{NLO Differential spectra}
1125: \label{sec:diffnlo}
1126: 
1127: In the course of an experimental analysis it is common practice to
1128: normalize the number of events generated in an event generator by a
1129: ``K-factor''.  This K-factor is generally taken to be the ratio of the
1130: NLO to LO inclusive cross section.  It is then assumed that turning on
1131: successive gluon radiation, called showering, in an event generator
1132: reproduces the correct shapes for the NLO distributions.  While this
1133: is a reasonable approximation for the soft radiation that accompanies
1134: the jets, it does not always reproduce the spectrum of additional
1135: well-separated hard jets \cite{Corcella:2000bw,Sjostrand:2001yu}, or
1136: their effect on the primary jets.  Since experimental reconstruction
1137: efficiencies depend on jet energies, it is important to have the most
1138: accurate prediction possible.
1139: 
1140: There are two main benefits of looking at the fully differential cross
1141: section.  The first is that this provides a check on the jet
1142: distributions that come from the event generators.  The second is that
1143: we see immediately whether the kinematic regions where perturbation
1144: theory breaks down are relevant to the measurable range of the
1145: distributions.  The shape of the transverse momentum is especially
1146: important in studies with $b$-tags, since the tagging efficiencies
1147: depend on this variable.
1148: 
1149: In Figs.~\ref{fig:ptt} and \ref{fig:ptb} we show the transverse
1150: momentum ($p_T$) distributions for the top-quark and bottom-jet,
1151: respectively, for $p\bar p\to \wprmp\!\to t\bar b$, and
1152: $m_{\wprm}=500$~GeV at run I of the Tevatron.  For comparison we plot
1153: both the NLO distributions and the LO distributions times a NLO
1154: K-factor of $1.29$.  The $b$-jet is reconstructed using a $k_T$
1155: cluster algorithm~\cite{Ellis:tq} to provide an infrared-safe way of
1156: combining partons.  We use a $k_T$ cone size of $\Delta R = 1$,
1157: similar to a fixed cone size of $0.7$.

1260: the effectiveness of $M_{t\bar b}$, the reconstructible signal over
1261: background may be a factor of 2 smaller than predicted with a LO
1262: calculation.

1271: The two distinguishing features of the \wpr cross section are that the
1272: $b$-jet and top-quark are each at a much larger transverse momentum
1273: than the dominant backgrounds, and there is a peak in the
1274: top-quark/antibottom-jet invariant mass distribution.  While an
1275: optimized phenomenological analysis of the $s$-channel
1276: single-top-quark production cross section at the level of
1277: Ref.~\cite{Stelzer:1998ni} is beyond the scope of this paper, we
1278: estimate the reach in \wpr mass using run I data in the following way:
1279: We begin with the recent limit on the $s$-channel single-top-quark
1280: cross section of $\sim 17$~pb \cite{Abazov:2001ns,Acosta:2001un}.
1281: Assuming that the \wpr boson adds directly to the standard model cross
1282: section, this immediately places a competitive bound of $m_{\wprm}
1283: \agt 380$--$410$~GeV (depending on the allowed decay modes).  To
1284: improve this bound, we note that the invariant mass $M_{Wb\bar b}$ of
1285: the dominant $Wb\bar b$ background ($B$) scales like $1/M^4_{Wb\bar
1286: b}$.  Hence, by reconstructing the \wpr invariant mass, and scaling
1287: the cross section limit by $\sqrt{B}$, we predict a $95\%$
1288: confidence-level limit of $m_{\wprm} \agt 525$--550~GeV should be
1289: attainable in a dedicated analysis of run I data.  In run II of the
1290: Tevatron the $s$-channel single-top-quark cross section will be
1291: measured to $\pm 20\%$ with 2~fb$^{-1}$ of integrated luminosity
1292: \cite{Stelzer:1998ni}.  Given the very low backgrounds at large
1293: invariant masses, limits of 800--900~GeV may be reachable for \wpr
1294: bosons with standard-model size couplings.

1296: \section{Conclusions}
1297: 
1298: We present a fully differential calculation of \wpr boson production
1299: and decay at next-to-leading order in QCD.  We demonstrate that the
1300: couplings of the \wpr to fermions factorize through NLO in the width,
1301: and in the complete two-to-two cross section.  Any model that contains
1302: a new charged-current gauge particle, with arbitrary vector and
1303: axial-vector couplings, is described by the analytic results of
1304: Secs.~\ref{sec:width} and \ref{sec:sigma}.  In particular, the
1305: completely differential NLO cross section may be used to predict jet
1306: distributions for a given model in terms of $|V^{\prime}_{f_if_j}|$,
1307: $R_t$, and $R_u$.  In most models, left-right mixing is either highly
1308: suppressed, or identically zero, which leads to a value of $R_u=0$.
1309: Hence, by calculating $R_t$, we may translate the results for right-
1310: or left-handed \wpr bosons, appearing in Secs.~\ref{sec:tottop} and
1311: \ref{sec:diffnlo}, into predictions for these models as well.
1312: 
1313: We use our calculation to estimate the effect of a left- or
1314: right-handed \wpr boson on the single-top-quark cross section.  We
1315: show that the dominant uncertainties in the theoretical prediction
1316: come from the top-quark mass, higher-order QCD, and the parton
1317: distribution functions.  In order to determine the PDF uncertainties,
1318: we propose the use of an improved modified tolerance method (MTM) that
1319: attains maximal sensitivity to the variance of the PDFs, and allows us
1320: to predict asymmetrical uncertainties.  We present the NLO transverse
1321: momentum and pseudorapidity distributions of the top-quark and
1322: bottom-jet.  We describe the effect of jet definitions on these
1323: distributions, and point out the strong sensitivity near the \wpr
1324: resonance region.  We show that the correlated effect of additional
1325: hard radiation on the reconstruction of the \wpr mass peak can be much
1326: greater than naively expected from the increase in the \wpr width.
1327: 
1328: We predict that the direct search limit on the mass of the \wpr boson
1329: may be improved by using data from runs I and II of the Fermilab
1330: Tevatron.  By reconstructing the top-quark/bottom-jet invariant mass
1331: $M_{tb}$ in the single-top-quark sample, a run I $95\%$
1332: confidence-level limit of $m_{\wprm} \agt 525$--550~GeV should be
1333: attainable for standard-model-like couplings.  At the end of run II,
1334: this limit may be pushed to 800--900~GeV.  The signal at the LHC
1335: should be large enough to reach limits of at least 3--4~TeV.  While
1336: these estimations are based on the known scaling of the backgrounds, a
1337: dedicated phenomenological analysis would be useful.
1338: 
1339: We conclude by applying our results to one specific example.  In the
1340: top-flavor model of Ref.~\cite{He:1999vp}, the left-handed coupling in
1341: the $\wprm$-$t$-$b$ vertex may be written as
1342: \beq
1343: g_L\sin\zeta\, V^L_{tb} = g\tan\phi\, V_{tb} \,.
1344: \eeq
1345: The coupling to leptons, or the first and second generation of quarks,
1346: can be written
1347: \beq
1348: g_L\sin\zeta\, V^L_{f_if_j} = g\cot\phi\, V_{f_if_j} \,,
1349: \eeq
1350: where $g$ is the standard model SU(2)$_L$ coupling, and $V_{f_if_j}$
1351: is the CKM matrix or diagonal, for quarks or leptons, respectively.
1352: For masses of around 500~GeV, the angle $\phi$ is restricted to be
1353: small \cite{Malkawi:1999sa}, $\sin^2\!\phi < 0.05$.  If we choose
1354: $\sin^2\!\phi = 0.05$, the branching ratio into top quarks is $99\%$;
1355: virtually all of the decays of the \wpr will be into top quarks.  The
1356: enhancement in branching fraction is exactly compensated by a decrease
1357: in production luminosity.  The single-top-quark cross section has $R_t
1358: = \tan^2\!\phi\, \cot^2\!\phi\, R_t^{\mathrm SM}$.  Thus, the direct
1359: search limit for this top-flavor model will be identical to the one
1360: derived with standard-model couplings.  If we wish to set a limit
1361: using a smaller value for $\sin^2\!\phi$, the \wpr width will be the
1362: limiting factor in the mass reconstruction, and we should reevaluate
1363: the jet distributions in that scenario.  By calculating
1364: $|V^{\prime}_{f_if_j}|$, $R_t$, and $R_u$, and using our
1365: next-to-leading order results, we may now accurately compare any model
1366: containing a \wpr boson to direct experimental searches.

\subsection{Parton distribution function uncertainties}
\label{sec:pdfu}

Because we are interested in heavy particles, the parton distribution
functions (PDFs) will be probed at large values of the proton's
momentum fraction.  Hence, as opposed to Drell-Yan or $s$-channel
single-top-quark production where the PDFs are well understood, we
expect the PDF uncertainty to play a significant role in the total
uncertainty of the cross section.  In order to estimate the effects of
this uncertainty we use a modification
\cite{Sullivan:2001ry,Nadolsky:2001yg} of the ``tolerance method''
implemented in the CTEQ6 PDFs \cite{Pumplin:2002vw}.

The tolerance method is based on diagonalization of the matrix of
second derivatives for $\chi^{2}$ (a Hessian matrix) near the minimum
of $\chi^{2}$ for the PDF fits \cite{Pumplin:2001ct}.  Since
$\chi^{2}$ is approximately parabolic near its minimum $\chi^{2}_{0}$,
hypersurfaces of constant $\chi^{2}$ are hyperellipses in the space of
the original 20 PDF parameters $\{a_{i}\}$.  These hyperellipses are
transformed into hyperspheres by a change of coordinates
$\{a_{i}\}\rightarrow \{z_{i}\},\, i=1,\dots ,20$.  The tolerance
method assumes that all acceptable PDF sets correspond to a $\chi^{2}$
that does not exceed their minimal value $\chi _{0}^{2}$ more than by
$T^{2}$.  As a result, the acceptable PDF sets have $\{z_{i}\}$ within
a sphere of the radius $T^{2}$ around $\{z_{i}(\chi _{0}^{2})\}\equiv
\{z_{i}^{0}\}$.  In principle, $T$ should be chosen to correspond to a
$1\sigma$ deviation of the fit.  However, for simplicity we present
results for $T=10$, as used by the CTEQ6M101 -- CTEQ6M140 PDF tables
given in Ref. \cite{Pumplin:2002vw}.

The PDF uncertainty for an observable $O$ is the maximal change in $O$
as a function of variables $\{z_{i}\}$ varying within the tolerance
hypersphere.  The CTEQ6 paper estimates the variation of $O$ by using
a master formula
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:tolmast}
\delta O=\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\sum^{20}_{i=1}\delta O_{i}^{2}},\mbox {\,
where\, }\delta O_{i}\equiv T\frac{\partial O}{\partial z_{i}}\approx
T\frac{O(z^{0}_{i}+t)-O(z^{0}_{i}-t)}{t} \;,
\end{equation}
and $t=10$ is a step in the space of $z_{i}$.  Here, $O(z_{1}^{0},\dots
,z_{i}^{0}\pm t,\dots ,z_{20}^{0})$ is denoted as $O(z_{i}^{0}\pm t)$.
Eq.~(\ref{eq:tolmast}) is a good approximation for the PDF fits, but is
less useful for observables, e.g.\ cross sections.

The difficulty with Eq.~(\ref{eq:tolmast}) is well exemplified for the
problem at hand by Fig.~\ref{fig:errasm}.  Here we see the uncertainty
for each of the 20 pairs of PDFs as a function of the parameters $z_i$
for $m_{\wprm} = 500$ GeV.  If we apply Eq.~(\ref{eq:tolmast}) we would
predict an uncertainty of $\pm 5.9\%$.  However,
$O(z^{0}_{i}+t)-O(z^{0}_{i}-t) \approx 0$ for nearly half of the
parameters, even though Fig.~\ref{fig:errasm} shows that these provide
a large deviation.  The uncertainty in Eq.~(\ref{eq:tolmast}) appears to
be more sensitive to $z_i$ which have a small absolute effect, but
happen to cause a shift in the prediction which changes sign, than to
large fluctuations.  This defect of the master formula is a result of
the simple observation that the PDF set that minimizes the uncertainty
in a given observable $O$ is not necessarily the same as the one that
minimizes the fit to the global data set.

\begin{figure}[tbh]
\epsfxsize=3.4in
\centerline{\epsfbox{tpdferr.ps}} 
\caption{Uncertainty in the cross section for $m_{\wprm} = 500$ GeV
for each pair of PDFs using CTEQ6M1xx.  Circles are odd PDF sets.
Squares are even PDF sets.\label{fig:errasm}}
\end{figure}

In order to obtain a better estimator of the uncertainty of a generic
observable $O$, we introduce \cite{Sullivan:2001ry,Nadolsky:2001yg} the
``modified tolerance method'' (MTM) master formula.  We define the maximum
positive and negative errors on an observable $O$ by
\begin{eqnarray}
\delta O_{+} & = & \frac{T}{t}\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{20}\Bigl( \max 
[\,O(z^{0}_{i}+t)-O(z_{i}^{0}),O(z^{0}_{i}-t)-O(z_{i}^{0}),0]\Bigr)^2}
\;,\label{eq:pdferra} \\
\delta O_{-} & = & \frac{T}{t}\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{20}\Bigl( \max 
[\,O(z_{i}^{0})-O(z^{0}_{i}+t),O(z_{i}^{0})-O(z^{0}_{i}-t),0]\Bigr)^2}
\; ,\label{eq:pdferr}
\end{eqnarray}
where the ``tolerance'' $T$ is the same scaling parameter that
determines the overall range of allowed variation of $\chi^2$, and we
use $T=t=10$ as in the CTEQ6 PDF sets.  In
Eqs.~(\ref{eq:pdferra}, \ref{eq:pdferr}) we sum the maximum deviations
on the observable in each of the parameter directions, and hence
retain both maximal sensitivity to the parameters that vary the most
and estimate the range of allowed values of the cross section.  Given
the case in Fig.~\ref{fig:errasm}, we determine that $m_{\wprm} = 500$
GeV has an uncertainty of ${+8.6}{-6.2}\%$ --- half again as large
on the high side as estimated by the CTEQ method.

\subsection{NLO Differential spectra}
\label{sec:diffnlo}

In the course of an experimental analysis it is common practice to
normalize the number of events generated in an event generator by a
``K-factor''.  This K-factor is generally taken to be the ratio of the
NLO to LO inclusive cross section.  It is then assumed that turning on
successive gluon radiation, called showering, in an event generator
reproduces the correct shapes for the NLO distributions.  While this
is a reasonable approximation for the soft radiation that accompanies
the jets, it does not always reproduce the spectrum of additional
well-separated hard jets \cite{Corcella:2000bw,Sjostrand:2001yu}, or
their effect on the primary jets.  Since experimental reconstruction
efficiencies depend on jet energies, it is important to have the most
accurate prediction possible.

There are two main benefits of looking at the fully differential cross
section.  The first is that this provides a check on the jet
distributions that come from the event generators.  The second is that
we see immediately whether the kinematic regions where perturbation
theory breaks down are relevant to the measurable range of the
distributions.  The shape of the transverse momentum is especially
important in studies with $b$-tags, since the tagging efficiencies
depend on this variable.

In Figs.~\ref{fig:ptt} and \ref{fig:ptb} we show the transverse
momentum ($p_T$) distributions for the top-quark and bottom-jet,
respectively, for $p\bar p\to \wprmp\!\to t\bar b$, and
$m_{\wprm}=500$~GeV at run I of the Tevatron.  For comparison we plot
both the NLO distributions and the LO distributions times a NLO
K-factor of $1.29$.  The $b$-jet is reconstructed using a $k_T$
cluster algorithm~\cite{Ellis:tq} to provide an infrared-safe way of
combining partons.  We use a $k_T$ cone size of $\Delta R = 1$,
similar to a fixed cone size of $0.7$.

going to higher orders, it may be possible to further improve the
shape in the resonance region by replacing the Breit-Wigner with a
more dynamical form \cite{Seymour:1995qg}.  While there may be minor
deviations at small transverse momentum due our choice of a massless
bottom quark, the cross section vanishes at low $p_{Tb}$, and $b$-jet
cannot be measured below about 10 GeV, so the effect will not be
visible in the experiments.  The pseudorapidity distributions of the

An important consideration is the effect of the choice of cone size on
the shape of the transverse momentum distributions.  In
Fig.~\ref{fig:rb}, we show the ratio of the $p_T$ distributions of the
$b$-jet for two common choices of $\Delta R=0.54$ and $1.35$ (which
are similar to fixed cones of size $0.4$ and $1.0$, respectively) to
our default choice of $1.0$.  When comparing distributions from event
generators with NLO calculations, we must use the same jet definition.
Otherwise, there can be a systematic shift in the shape of the
distributions of $10$--$20\%$.  This size of this effect is
potentially larger than the effect of the jet-energy resolution on the
reconstruction of jet shapes.

The overall effect of the choice of cone size is only important for
\wpr production right near resonance.  The cross section is fairly
small at lower transverse momentum, and thus changes in the shape in
that region are not relevant.  The effect at low $p_T$ is further
suppressed in an experiment, because $b$-tagging efficiency tends to
be smaller at low $p_T$ as well.  In Fig.~\ref{fig:rptb} we show the
effect of different cone sizes on the $p_{Tb}$ spectrum near the its
peak at $\sim 215$~GeV, which corresponds to a 500~GeV \wpr resonance.
Experimental analyses will concentrate on this resonant region.
Hence, a mismatch of jet definitions could cause a systematic mistake
in the comparison to the theoretical cross section of as much as $\pm
20\%$.

While the individual distributions for the \wpr boson are important,
in an experimental analysis we want to fit for the mass of the \wpr
boson.  A likely strategy to find the \wpr is to look for a peak in
invariant mass distribution $M_{t\bar b}$ of the
top-quark/antibottom-jet pair.  We do not perform a full analysis
here, but simply show in Fig.~\ref{fig:mtb} the $M_{t\bar b}$
distributions for $m_{W^{\prime}} = 500$~GeV.  The LO cross section is
shown times the standard K-factor, but is divided by 2 to fit on the
figure.  While the central value of the peak has not shifted by much,
there is a very large tail below the mass of the \wpr boson.  Roughly
half of the cross section is below the peak predicted at LO.  Hard
radiation at NLO has a much larger effect on the correlated
distributions than we might naively expect from the $4\%$ increase in
the width.  Almost $2/3$ of the LO distribution falls in a mass window
of $500\pm 10$ GeV, but only $1/2$ of the NLO distribution falls in a
mass window twice as wide, $500\pm 20$ GeV.  Hence, when considering
the effectiveness of $M_{t\bar b}$, the reconstructible signal over
background may be a factor of 2 smaller than predicted with a LO
calculation.

\caption{Invariant mass distribution $M_{t\bar b}$ at NLO, and LO
times a K-factor, for $m_{W^{\prime}}=500$~GeV.\label{fig:mtb}}
\end{figure}

The two distinguishing features of the \wpr cross section are that the
$b$-jet and top-quark are each at a much larger transverse momentum
than the dominant backgrounds, and there is a peak in the
top-quark/antibottom-jet invariant mass distribution.  While an
optimized phenomenological analysis of the $s$-channel
single-top-quark production cross section at the level of
Ref.~\cite{Stelzer:1998ni} is beyond the scope of this paper, we
estimate the reach in \wpr mass using run I data in the following way:
We begin with the recent limit on the $s$-channel single-top-quark
cross section of $\sim 17$~pb \cite{Abazov:2001ns,Acosta:2001un}.
Assuming that the \wpr boson adds directly to the standard model cross
section, this immediately places a competitive bound of $m_{\wprm}
\agt 380$--$410$~GeV (depending on the allowed decay modes).  To
improve this bound, we note that the invariant mass $M_{Wb\bar b}$ of
the dominant $Wb\bar b$ background ($B$) scales like $1/M^4_{Wb\bar
b}$.  Hence, by reconstructing the \wpr invariant mass, and scaling
the cross section limit by $\sqrt{B}$, we predict a $95\%$
confidence-level limit of $m_{\wprm} \agt 525$--550~GeV should be
attainable in a dedicated analysis of run I data.  In run II of the
Tevatron the $s$-channel single-top-quark cross section will be
measured to $\pm 20\%$ with 2~fb$^{-1}$ of integrated luminosity
\cite{Stelzer:1998ni}.  Given the very low backgrounds at large
invariant masses, limits of 800--900~GeV may be reachable for \wpr
bosons with standard-model size couplings.

\section{Conclusions}

We present a fully differential calculation of \wpr boson production
and decay at next-to-leading order in QCD.  We demonstrate that the
couplings of the \wpr to fermions factorize through NLO in the width,
and in the complete two-to-two cross section.  Any model that contains
a new charged-current gauge particle, with arbitrary vector and
axial-vector couplings, is described by the analytic results of
Secs.~\ref{sec:width} and \ref{sec:sigma}.  In particular, the
completely differential NLO cross section may be used to predict jet
distributions for a given model in terms of $|V^{\prime}_{f_if_j}|$,
$R_t$, and $R_u$.  In most models, left-right mixing is either highly
suppressed, or identically zero, which leads to a value of $R_u=0$.
Hence, by calculating $R_t$, we may translate the results for right-
or left-handed \wpr bosons, appearing in Secs.~\ref{sec:tottop} and
\ref{sec:diffnlo}, into predictions for these models as well.

We use our calculation to estimate the effect of a left- or
right-handed \wpr boson on the single-top-quark cross section.  We
show that the dominant uncertainties in the theoretical prediction
come from the top-quark mass, higher-order QCD, and the parton
distribution functions.  In order to determine the PDF uncertainties,
we propose the use of an improved modified tolerance method (MTM) that
attains maximal sensitivity to the variance of the PDFs, and allows us
to predict asymmetrical uncertainties.  We present the NLO transverse
momentum and pseudorapidity distributions of the top-quark and
bottom-jet.  We describe the effect of jet definitions on these
distributions, and point out the strong sensitivity near the \wpr
resonance region.  We show that the correlated effect of additional
hard radiation on the reconstruction of the \wpr mass peak can be much
greater than naively expected from the increase in the \wpr width.

We predict that the direct search limit on the mass of the \wpr boson
may be improved by using data from runs I and II of the Fermilab
Tevatron.  By reconstructing the top-quark/bottom-jet invariant mass
$M_{tb}$ in the single-top-quark sample, a run I $95\%$
confidence-level limit of $m_{\wprm} \agt 525$--550~GeV should be
attainable for standard-model-like couplings.  At the end of run II,
this limit may be pushed to 800--900~GeV.  The signal at the LHC
should be large enough to reach limits of at least 3--4~TeV.  While
these estimations are based on the known scaling of the backgrounds, a
dedicated phenomenological analysis would be useful.

We conclude by applying our results to one specific example.  In the
top-flavor model of Ref.~\cite{He:1999vp}, the left-handed coupling in
the $\wprm$-$t$-$b$ vertex may be written as
\beq
g_L\sin\zeta\, V^L_{tb} = g\tan\phi\, V_{tb} \,.
\eeq
The coupling to leptons, or the first and second generation of quarks,
can be written
\beq
g_L\sin\zeta\, V^L_{f_if_j} = g\cot\phi\, V_{f_if_j} \,,
\eeq
where $g$ is the standard model SU(2)$_L$ coupling, and $V_{f_if_j}$
is the CKM matrix or diagonal, for quarks or leptons, respectively.
For masses of around 500~GeV, the angle $\phi$ is restricted to be
small \cite{Malkawi:1999sa}, $\sin^2\!\phi < 0.05$.  If we choose
$\sin^2\!\phi = 0.05$, the branching ratio into top quarks is $99\%$;
virtually all of the decays of the \wpr will be into top quarks.  The
enhancement in branching fraction is exactly compensated by a decrease
in production luminosity.  The single-top-quark cross section has $R_t
= \tan^2\!\phi\, \cot^2\!\phi\, R_t^{\mathrm SM}$.  Thus, the direct
search limit for this top-flavor model will be identical to the one
derived with standard-model couplings.  If we wish to set a limit
using a smaller value for $\sin^2\!\phi$, the \wpr width will be the
limiting factor in the mass reconstruction, and we should reevaluate
the jet distributions in that scenario.  By calculating
$|V^{\prime}_{f_if_j}|$, $R_t$, and $R_u$, and using our
next-to-leading order results, we may now accurately compare any model
containing a \wpr boson to direct experimental searches.

52: (* v1.2: Set FeynmanGauge=True as default.                                   *)
53: (*       Set Gluonic ghosts to be included in both gauges.                   *)

714:     yl[ff1, ff3] LLbar[sp, ii, ff1].lR [sp, ff3] Phi[ii] -

722:   LGh1 = -ghBbar.del[DC[ghB,mu],mu];
723:   LGhw = -ghWibar[ii].del[DC[ghWi[ii],mu],mu];
724:   LGhs = -ghGbar[ii].del[DC[ghG[ii],mu],mu];

727:   (* phi1 and phi2 are the real degrees of freedom of GP *)
728:   (* Vectorize transforms a doublet in a vector in the phi-basis, i.e. the basis of real degrees of freedom *)
729:   gh    = {ghB, ghWi[1], ghWi[2], ghWi[3]};
730:   ghbar = {ghBbar, ghWibar[1], ghWibar[2], ghWibar[3]};

733:   doublet0 = {0, vev/Sqrt[2]};
734:   Vectorize[{a_, b_}]:= Simplify[{Sqrt[2] Re[Expand[a]], Sqrt[2] Im[Expand[a]], Sqrt[2] Re[Expand[b]], Sqrt[2] Im[Expand[b]]}/.{Im[_]->0, Re[num_]->num}];

737: 
738: ExpandIndices[ LGhs + If[FeynmanGauge, LGh1 + LGhw + LGhphi,0], FlavorExpand->SU2W]];
739: 
740: LSM:= LGauge + LFermions + LHiggs + LYukawa + LGhost;

3: 
4: Every rule encodes one construct that broke a compile, a FeynRules check or a
5: MadGraph import in the benchmark (prompt_addendum_v3.txt rules 9-15 and the
6: repair-loop taxonomy). A lint runs in milliseconds on the text; the compile it
7: predicts takes up to 900 s.
8: 
9: Each finding carries the STAGE it predicts:
10:   compile  - FeynRules will not load or will not finish the model
11:   checks   - the model loads but a consistency check fails
12:   mg5      - the UFO is written but MadGraph rejects it
13:   harness  - the validation harness cannot pick the total Lagrangian
14:   warn     - FeynRules warns; the run may still pass
15: 
16: Library: ``lint_text(text) -> list[Finding]``. CLI: ``fr_lint.py file.fr``.
17: """

77: def strip_comments(text: str) -> str:
78:     out, depth, i = [], 0, 0
79:     while i < len(text):
80:         if text.startswith("(*", i):
81:             depth += 1
82:             i += 2
83:             continue
84:         if text.startswith("*)", i) and depth:
85:             depth -= 1
86:             i += 2
87:             continue
88:         if depth == 0:
89:             out.append(text[i])
90:         elif text[i] == "\n":

92:         i += 1

96: def _matching(text: str, open_idx: int) -> int:
97:     depth = 0
98:     pairs = {"{": "}", "[": "]", "(": ")"}
99:     closes = set(pairs.values())
100:     for j in range(open_idx, len(text)):
101:         ch = text[j]
102:         if ch in pairs:
103:             depth += 1
104:         elif ch in closes:
105:             depth -= 1
106:             if depth == 0:

119: def _entries(block: str) -> List[Dict]:
120:     """Top-level `Head == { ... }` entries of a M$ block."""
121:     out = []

123:         end = _matching(block, m.end() - 1)
124:         body = block[m.end():end]
125:         out.append({"head": m.group(1), "body": body, "pos": m.start()})
126:     return out
127: 
128: 
129: def _prop(body: str, key: str) -> Optional[str]:
130:     m = re.search(rf"\b{key}\s*->\s*", body)
131:     if not m:
132:         return None
133:     rest = body[m.end():]
134:     if rest.startswith("{"):
135:         return rest[: _matching(rest, 0) + 1]
136:     mm = re.match(r"[^,}\n]+", rest)
137:     return mm.group(0).strip() if mm else None

139: 
140: def _is_kin_name(name: str) -> bool:
141:     return bool(re.search(r"kin|Kin|KIN|free|Free|Gauge|gauge", name))
142: 
143: 
144: def term_defs(text: str) -> List[Dict]:
145:     starts = [(m.group(1), m.start()) for m in re.finditer(r"^(L\w+)\s*:?=", text, re.M)]
146:     stops = [m.start() for m in re.finditer(r"^(?:M\$\w+\s*=|L\w+\s*:?=|\w+\s*=\s*\{)", text, re.M)]
147:     out = []
148:     for name, s in starts:
149:         e = min([x for x in stops if x > s] + [len(text)])
150:         out.append({"name": name, "body": text[s:e], "line": text[:s].count("\n") + 1})
151:     return out
152: 
153: 
154: def _line_of(text: str, needle: str) -> Optional[int]:
155:     i = text.find(needle)
156:     return text[:i].count("\n") + 1 if i >= 0 else None

158:

"""Deterministic lints for an agent-written FeynRules add-on (.fr) file.

Every rule encodes one construct that broke a compile, a FeynRules check or a
MadGraph import in the benchmark (prompt_addendum_v3.txt rules 9-15 and the

80:     return {k: v for k, v in d.items() if k not in _REP_LABELS}
81: 
82: 
83: def _reserved_mass_width_names(particles) -> set:
84:     """Mass/width parameter names FeynRules auto-declares from particle Mass/Width
85:     specs. Declaring them again in M$Parameters double-defines the name in the UFO
86:     (MadGraph InvalidModel), so the renderer drops those duplicates."""
87:     names: set = set()
88:     for p in particles or []:
89:         for spec in (getattr(p, "mass", None), getattr(p, "width", None)):
90:             if spec is None:
91:                 continue
92:             if getattr(spec, "sym", None):
93:                 names.add(spec.sym)
94:             for sub, _val in (getattr(spec, "members", None) or []):
95:                 names.add(sub)
96:     return names
97: 
98: 
99: def _is_internal_param(p) -> bool:
100:     """Internal/derived parameters carry a formula (Definitions) that FeynRules
101:     cannot auto-create from a particle Mass/Width spec, so they must stay in
102:     M$Parameters even when named like a mass/width (e.g. a computed decay width
103:     Width -> {WV1, Internal}). Only plain External duplicates are dropped."""
104:     if getattr(p, "definitions", None):
105:         return True
106:     return "internal" in str(getattr(p, "parameter_type", "")).lower()
107: 
108: 
109: def _qn(d: dict) -> str:
110:     return "{" + ", ".join(f"{k} -> {v}" for k, v in _additive_qns(d).items()) + "}"
111: 
112: 
113: def _interaction_order(t: Tuple[str, int]) -> str:
114:     return f"{{{t[0]}, {t[1]}}}"
115: 
116: 
117: def _mw_value(v):
118:     """Normalize a mass/width value. FeynRules' ``Automatic`` width is computed
119:     only when AddDecays is on — which is off for us (broken on Wolfram >=15), so
120:     it leaks the literal ``Automatic`` into the UFO and MadGraph fails with
121:     ``name 'Automatic' is not defined``. Emit a numeric placeholder instead;
122:     MadGraph's compute_widths recovers the real width from the model."""
123:     return "1." if str(v).strip().lower() == "automatic" else v
124: 
125: 
126: def _mass(m: MassSpec) -> str:
127:     if m.massless:
128:         return "0"
129:     if m.members:
130:         parts = [m.sym]
131:         for sub, val in m.members:
132:             val = _mw_value(val)
133:             parts.append(f"{{{sub}, {val}}}" if val is not None else f"{{{sub}}}")
134:         return "{" + ", ".join(parts) + "}"
135:     if m.value is not None:
136:         return f"{{{m.sym}, {_mw_value(m.value)}}}"
137:     return f"{{{m.sym}}}"
138: 
139: 
140: def _reps(reps: Sequence[Tuple[str, str]]) -> str:
141:     if len(reps) == 1:
142:         r, s = reps[0]
143:         return f"{{{r}, {s}}}"
144:     return "{" + ", ".join(f"{{{r}, {s}}}" for r, s in reps) + "}"
145: 
146: 
147: def _assoc(pairs: List[Tuple[str, Optional[str]]], indent: str = "    ") -> str:
148:     """Render ``{ Key -> val, ... }``, dropping entries whose value is None."""
149:     kept = [(k, v) for k, v in pairs if v is not None]
150:     if not kept:
151:         return "{}"
152:     inner = ",\n".join(f"{indent}{k} -> {v}" for k, v in kept)
153:     close_indent = indent[:-2] if len(indent) >= 2 else ""
154:     return "{\n" + inner + "\n" + close_indent + "}"
155: 
156: 
157: # ------------------------------ blocks ------------------------------- #
158: 
159: 
160: def render_information(info) -> str:
161:     pairs = [
162:         ("Authors", _strlist(info.authors)),
163:         ("Version", _quote(info.version)),
164:         ("Date", _quote(info.date)),
165:         ("Institutions", _strlist(info.institutions) if info.institutions else None),
166:         ("Emails", _strlist(info.emails) if info.emails else None),
167:     ]
168:     return "M$Information = " + _assoc(pairs, indent="  ") + ";"
169: 
170: 
171: def _render_gauge_group(g: GaugeGroup) -> str:
172:     pairs: List[Tuple[str, Optional[str]]] = [
173:         ("Abelian", _bool(g.abelian)),
174:         ("CouplingConstant", g.coupling_constant),
175:         ("GaugeBoson", g.gauge_boson),
176:         ("Charge", g.charge),
177:         ("StructureConstant", g.structure_constant),
178:         ("Representations", _reps(g.representations) if g.representations else None),
179:         ("SymmetricTensor", g.symmetric_tensor),
180:         (
181:             "Definitions",
182:             ("{" + ", ".join(g.definitions) + "}") if g.definitions else None,
183:         ),
184:     ]
185:     return f"  {g.name} == " + _assoc(pairs, indent="    ")
186: 
187: 
188: def render_gauge_groups(groups: List[GaugeGroup]) -> str:
189:     entries = ",\n".join(_render_gauge_group(g) for g in groups)
190:     return "M$GaugeGroups = {\n" + entries + "\n};"
191: 
192: 
193: def render_index_decls(decls: List[IndexDecl]) -> str:
194:     lines: List[str] = []
195:     for d in decls:
196:         if d.range_kind.value == "Range":
197:             rng = f"Range[{d.size}]"
198:         else:
199:             rng = f"{d.range_kind.value}[Range[{d.size}]]"
200:         lines.append(f"IndexRange[Index[{d.name}]] = {rng};")
201:     for d in decls:
202:         if d.style_symbol:
203:             lines.append(f"IndexStyle[{d.name}, {d.style_symbol}];")
204:     return "\n".join(lines)
205: 
206: 
207: def _render_parameter(p: Parameter) -> str:
208:     pairs: List[Tuple[str, Optional[str]]] = [
209:         ("ParameterType", p.parameter_type.value if p.parameter_type else None),
210:     ]
211:     if p.is_tensor:
212:         pairs.append(
213:             (
214:                 "Value",
215:                 ("{" + ", ".join(r.render() for r in p.value_rules) + "}")
216:                 if p.value_rules
217:                 else None,
218:             )
219:         )
220:         pairs.append(("Indices", _indices(p.indices)))
221:     else:
222:         pairs.append(("Value", p.value))
223:     pairs += [
224:         ("ComplexParameter", _bool(p.complex) if p.complex is not None else None),
225:         ("BlockName", p.block_name),
226:         ("OrderBlock", str(p.order_block) if p.order_block is not None else None),
227:         (
228:             "InteractionOrder",
229:             _interaction_order(p.interaction_order) if p.interaction_order else None,
230:         ),
231:         (
232:             "Definitions",
233:             ("{" + ", ".join(r.render() for r in p.definitions) + "}")
234:             if p.definitions
235:             else None,
236:         ),
237:         ("ParameterName", p.parameter_name),
238:         ("TensorClass", p.tensor_class),
239:         ("Unitary", _bool(p.unitary) if p.unitary is not None else None),
240:         ("Hermitian", _bool(p.hermitian) if p.hermitian is not None else None),
241:         ("Orthogonal", _bool(p.orthogonal) if p.orthogonal is not None else None),
242:         (
243:             "AllowSummation",
244:             _bool(p.allow_summation) if p.allow_summation is not None else None,
245:         ),
246:         # TeX is a LaTeX label; render it as a quoted Mathematica string with
247:         # backslashes escaped ("\\Gamma_U"), else a raw value like \Gamma_U is a
248:         # Mathematica syntax error that aborts the whole M$Parameters block.
249:         ("TeX", _quote(p.tex) if p.tex else None),
250:         ("Description", _quote(p.description) if p.description else None),
251:     ]
252:     return f"  {p.name} == " + _assoc(pairs, indent="    ")
253: 
254: 
255: def render_parameters(params: List[Parameter]) -> str:
256:     entries = ",\n".join(_render_parameter(p) for p in params)
257:     return "M$Parameters = {\n" + entries + "\n};"
258: 
259: 
260: def _render_particle(p: ParticleClass) -> str:
261:     pairs: List[Tuple[str, Optional[str]]] = [
262:         ("ClassName", p.class_name),
263:         ("SelfConjugate", _bool(p.self_conjugate)),
264:         (
265:             "ClassMembers",
266:             ("{" + ", ".join(p.class_members) + "}") if p.class_members else None,
267:         ),
268:         ("Indices", _indices(p.indices) if p.indices else None),
269:         ("FlavorIndex", p.flavor_index),
270:         ("Mass", _mass(p.mass) if p.mass else None),
271:         ("Width", _mass(p.width) if p.width else None),
272:         ("QuantumNumbers",
273:          _qn(p.quantum_numbers) if _additive_qns(p.quantum_numbers or {}) else None),
274:         ("PDG", _pdg(p.pdg) if p.pdg is not None else None),
275:         ("ParticleName", _name_field(p.particle_name) if p.particle_name else None),
276:         (
277:             "AntiParticleName",
278:             _name_field(p.antiparticle_name) if p.antiparticle_name else None,
279:         ),
280:         ("FullName", _name_field(p.full_name) if p.full_name else None),
281:         (
282:             "PropagatorLabel",
283:             _name_field(p.propagator_label) if p.propagator_label else None,
284:         ),
285:         ("PropagatorType", p.propagator_type.value if p.propagator_type else None),
286:         ("PropagatorArrow", p.propagator_arrow.value if p.propagator_arrow else None),
287:         ("Ghost", p.ghost),
288:         ("Goldstone", p.goldstone),
289:         ("Chirality", p.chirality),
290:         ("MajoranaPhase", p.majorana_phase),
291:         (
292:             "WeylComponents",
293:             ("{" + ", ".join(p.weyl_components) + "}") if p.weyl_components else None,
294:         ),
295:         ("Unphysical", _bool(True) if p.unphysical else None),
296:         (
297:             "Definitions",
298:             ("{" + ", ".join(p.definitions) + "}") if p.definitions else None,
299:         ),
300:     ]
301:     return f"  {p.class_label} == " + _assoc(pairs, indent="    ")
302: 
303: 
304: def render_classes(particles: List[ParticleClass]) -> str:
305:     entries = ",\n".join(_render_particle(p) for p in particles)
306:     return "M$ClassesDescription = {\n" + entries + "\n};"
307: 
308: 
309: def render_model(model: FeynRulesModel) -> str:
310:     """Render a validated FeynRulesModel to a complete ``.fr`` string."""
311:     sections: List[str] = [render_information(model.info)]
312: 
313:     if model.interaction_order_hierarchy:
314:         ih = ", ".join(_interaction_order(t) for t in model.interaction_order_hierarchy)
315:         sections.append("M$InteractionOrderHierarchy = {" + ih + "};")
316:     if model.interaction_order_limit:
317:         il = ", ".join(_interaction_order(t) for t in model.interaction_order_limit)
318:         sections.append("M$InteractionOrderLimit = {" + il + "};")
319:     if model.feynman_gauge is not None:
320:         sections.append(f"FeynmanGauge = {_bool(model.feynman_gauge)};")
321:     if model.vevs:
322:         vv = ", ".join(f"{{{f}, {v}}}" for f, v in model.vevs)
323:         sections.append("M$vevs = {" + vv + "};")
324: 
325:     for raw in model.raw_preamble:
326:         sections.append(raw)
327: 
328:     if model.index_decls:
329:         sections.append(render_index_decls(model.index_decls))
330:     if model.gauge_groups:
331:         sections.append(render_gauge_groups(model.gauge_groups))
332:     if model.parameters:
333:         # FeynRules auto-declares the mass/width parameters named in each
334:         # particle's Mass/Width spec. Re-declaring them in M$Parameters makes the
335:         # UFO define the name twice, which MadGraph rejects ("name X define
336:         # multiple time"). Drop those duplicates; keep genuine couplings.
337:         reserved = _reserved_mass_width_names(model.particles)
338:         params = [p for p in model.parameters
339:                   if p.name not in reserved or _is_internal_param(p)]
340:         if params:
341:             sections.append(render_parameters(params))
342:     if model.particles:
343:         sections.append(render_classes(model.particles))
344:     for field, expr in model.gauge_xi:
345:         sections.append(f"GaugeXi[{field}] = {expr};")
346: 
347:     for raw in model.raw_blocks:
348:         sections.append(raw)
349: 
350:     for t in model.lagrangian_terms:
351:         op = ":=" if t.delayed else "="
352:         # Defensive: some (LLM-produced) expressions already carry a leading
353:         # assignment operator ("= ..." or ":= ..."); strip it so we don't emit a
354:         # duplicated operator (e.g. "L := := Block[...]").
355:         rhs = t.expression.lstrip()
356:         for lead in (":=", "="):
357:             if rhs.startswith(lead):
358:                 rhs = rhs[len(lead):].lstrip()
359:                 break
360:         sections.append(f"{t.name} {op} {rhs};")
361: 
362:     env = Environment(
363:         loader=FileSystemLoader(_TEMPLATE_DIR),
364:         autoescape=select_autoescape(enabled_extensions=(), default=False),
365:         keep_trailing_newline=True,
366:     )
367:     template = env.get_template("model.fr.j2")
368:     return template.render(model_name=model.model_name, body="\n\n".join(sections))

18: \title{Fully differential $W^\prime$ production and decay at next-to-leading
19: order in QCD}
20: 
21: \author{Zack Sullivan}
22: \address{Theoretical Physics Department, Fermi National
23: Accelerator Laboratory, Batavia, IL, 60510-0500}
24: 
25: \date{July 23, 2002}
26: 
27: \maketitle
28: 
29: \begin{abstract}
30: We present the fully differential production and decay of a $W^\prime$
31: boson, with arbitrary vector and axial-vector couplings, to any final
32: state at next-to-leading order in QCD.  We demonstrate a complete
33: factorization of couplings at next-to-leading order in both the
34: partial width of the $W^\prime$ boson, and in the full two-to-two
35: cross section.  We provide numerical predictions for the contribution
36: of a $W^\prime$ boson to single-top-quark production, and separate
37: results based on whether the mass of the right-handed neutrino $\nu_R$
38: is light enough for the leptonic decay channel to be open.  The
39: single-top-quark analysis will allow for an improved direct $W^\prime$
40: mass limit of 525--550~GeV using data from run I of the Fermilab
41: Tevatron.  We propose a modified tolerance method for estimating
42: parton distribution function uncertainties in cross sections.
43: \end{abstract}
44: 
45: \section{Introduction}
46: 
47: Since the introduction of the standard model, many extensions have
48: been proposed that involve enhanced gauge symmetries.  One common
49: feature of these models is the prediction of additional gauge bosons,
50: generically called \wpr and $Z^\prime$ bosons.  In non-universal and
51: top-flavor models, the \wpr gauge boson arises from a new SU(2)$_L$
52: sector that distinguishes between generations of fermions
53: \cite{Li:nk,Malkawi:1996fs,Muller:1996dj}, and may treat quarks and
54: leptons differently \cite{Georgi:1989ic,Georgi:1989xz,He:1999vp}.  The
55: \wpr boson could be the lowest Kaluza-Klein mode of the $W$ boson
56: \cite{Datta:2000gm}, or a heavy mass eigenstate in non-commuting
57: extended technicolor \cite{Chivukula:1995gu}.  In a left-right
58: symmetric model the \wpr and standard-model $W$ bosons are remnants of
59: a broken ${\mathrm SU(2)}_L \times {\mathrm SU(2)}_R$ symmetry
60: \cite{Pati:1974yy,Mohapatra:1974hk,Mohapatra:1974gc,Senjanovic:1975rk}.
61: The resulting left-right mixing may be naturally suppressed by
62: orbifold breaking of the left-right symmetry \cite{Mimura:2002te}, or
63: by supersymmetric interactions \cite{Cvetic:1983su}.  While indirect
64: bounds may be placed on the masses and couplings of these various \wpr
65: bosons within the context of their explicit theories, it is always
66: advantageous to search for these new particles directly.  In order to
67: facilitate a direct experimental search, and to achieve the most
68: general contact with theory, we calculate the fully differential
69: next-to-leading order cross section for the production and decay of a
70: \wpr boson to any final state with arbitrary vector and axial-vector
71: couplings.
72: 
73: The most general Lorentz invariant Lagrangian describing the coupling
74: of a \wpr to fermions may be written as
75: \beq
76: {\cal L} = \frac{g}{\sqrt{2}} \overline{f}_i\gamma_\mu \bigl(
77: C^R_{f_if_j} P_R + C^L_{f_if_j} P_L \bigr) W^{\prime} f_j +
78: \mathrm{H.c.} \,, \label{eq:genlan}
79: \eeq
80: where $P_{R,L}=(1\pm \gamma_5)/2$, $g$ is the standard model SU(2)$_L$
81: coupling, and the $C^{R,L}_{f_if_j}$ are arbitrary couplings that
82: differ for quarks and leptons.  For a standard model $W$ boson,
83: $C^R=0$, and $C^L$ is either the Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa matrix or
84: diagonal, for quarks or leptons, respectively.
85: 
86: Most experimental searches have concentrated on \wpr bosons that decay
87: via a purely left- or right-handed current.  In order to make contact
88: with these results, we rewrite Eq.~(\ref{eq:genlan}) in the notation
89: typical of left-right symmetric models as \cite{Langacker:1989xa}
90: \beq
91: {\cal L} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \overline{f}_i\gamma_\mu \bigl( g_R
92: e^{i\omega} \cos\zeta\, V^R_{f_if_j} P_R + g_L \sin\zeta\, V^L_{f_if_j}
93: P_L\bigr) W^{\prime} f_j + \mathrm{H.c.} \,, \label{eq:lagrangian}
94: \eeq
95: where $\zeta$ is a left-right mixing angle, and $\omega$ is a
96: CP-violating phase that can be absorbed into $V^R$.  In this notation,
97: $g_{R(L)}$ are the right (left) gauge couplings, and
98: $V^{R,L}_{f_if_j}$ are generalized Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa (GCKM)
99: matrices.  In models where the $W$ and \wpr mix, the mixing angle
100: $\zeta$ is usually constrained to be small ($|\zeta|<$ a few $\times
101: 10^{-5}$--$10^{-2}$ \cite{Groom:in}).  Hence, the search for purely
102: right- or left-handed states appears well motivated.
103: 
104: Many direct searches for \wpr bosons have been performed at hadron
105: colliders.  Most experimental analyses have considered left- or
106: right-handed \wpr bosons, with standard-model-like couplings, that
107: decay into leptonic final states.  Left-handed $W^\prime_L$ bosons, or
108: right-handed $W^\prime_R$ bosons in which the decay into a
109: right-handed neutrino $\nu_R$ is kinematically allowed, are
110: constrained to have masses $m_{\wprm} > 786$~GeV
111: \cite{Arnison:1983zy,Arnison:ut,Ansari:1987ch,Albajar:1988ka,Abe:1994zg,Abachi:1995yi,Abe:1999gz,Affolder:2001gr}.
112: If $m_{\nu_R} \agt m_{\wprm}$ the decay to $\nu_R$ is not allowed,
113: and the right-handed $W^\prime_R$ bosons are only directly constrained
114: by peak searches in the dijet data.  Unless the \wpr has greatly
115: enhanced couplings to light quarks, the dijet data are limited by QCD
116: backgrounds to providing a mass limit of $420$~GeV
117: \cite{Alitti:1990kw,Alitti:1993pn,Abe:1997hm}.
118: 
119: The only final state not measured by one of the experiments listed
120: above involves the decay of a \wpr to a single top quark.  In
121: Refs.~\cite{Simmons:1996ws,Tait:1997fe} it was pointed out that a
122: deviation of measured the single-top-quark cross section from the
123: standard model prediction could be evidence of a new gauge
124: interaction.  In the context of models with \wpr bosons, we wish to
125: take this one step further, and propose that the experiments search
126: for an explicit \wpr mass peak in the $s$-channel single-top-quark
127: sample.  We examine just how large the cross section into single top
128: quarks can be at the Fermilab Tevatron and Large Hadron Collider (LHC)
129: as a function of \wpr mass, and determine how enhanced or suppressed
130: couplings enter into the measurable cross section after cuts.  We also
131: determine the next-to-leading order distributions of the final-state
132: jets to estimate the effect on the reconstruction of the \wpr mass
133: peak.
134: 
135: A \wpr boson that propagates in the $s$-channel appears very similar
136: to Drell-Yan production.  We might be tempted to use the
137: next-to-next-to-leading order (NNLO) predictions for Drell-Yan
138: \cite{Hamberg:1990np} (or the updates in
139: Ref.~\cite{Harlander:2002wh}).  However, these calculations are not
140: adequate to predict the cross section for \wpr bosons which decay to
141: quarks.  There are two reasons for this.  The first problem is that
142: the final state effects are very large.  Not only are there large QCD
143: corrections to the quark final state, but the top-quark mass has a
144: large effect on the branching fraction when it is in the final state.
145: The second reason is that there are initial- and final-state
146: interference terms that arise at NNLO that are of an unknown size.
147: (Pure QCD processes also interfere at NNLO, e.g.\ with $u\bar d \to
148: u\bar d$ via the exchange of two gluons.)  Therefore, we cannot simply
149: take the NNLO production as calculated and append a Breit-Wigner
150: propagator that uses leading or next-to-leading order widths.
151: Instead, we perform the complete calculation at next-to-leading order.
152: 
153: We organize the paper as follows.  In Sec.~\ref{sec:width} we
154: calculate the partial widths into leptons or quarks, including the
155: effects of the top-quark mass, for the \wpr boson using arbitrary
156: vector and axial-vector couplings at next-to-leading order (NLO) in
157: QCD.  We demonstrate that the couplings factorize, and present some
158: numerical results for partial widths and branching fractions into a
159: top-quark final state.  In Sec.~\ref{sec:sigma} we calculate the fully
160: differential production and decay of a \wpr into any final state at
161: NLO in QCD.  We present numerical results for the single-top-quark
162: production cross section via $s$-channel exchange of a \wpr boson.  We
163: asses all theoretical uncertainties, and propose a modification of the
164: tolerance method for calculating parton distribution function
165: uncertainties.  Finally, we present the NLO jet distributions, discuss
166: the effect of jet definitions on these distributions, and estimate the
167: limits that may be placed on the \wpr mass using data from run I and
168: run II of the Fermilab Tevatron.
169: 
170: \section{Next-to-leading order width}
171: \label{sec:width}
172: 
173: We divide our evaluation of the \wpr width into three terms that
174: depend on the final decay products:
175: \beq
176: \Gamma_{\mathrm tot}(\wprm) = \Gamma (\wprm\to t{\bar q}^\prime)
177: +\Gamma (\wprm\to q{\bar q}^\prime) + \Gamma (\wprm\to l\bar\nu) \,.
178: \label{eq:widfact}
179: \eeq
180: We separate the partial widths containing a top quark from those
181: containing only massless quarks so that we may retain an explicit
182: top-quark mass dependence in the width.
183: 
184: While the large number of couplings in Eq.~(\ref{eq:lagrangian})
185: appears daunting, a factorization of the couplings occurs in the
186: partial widths of Eq.~(\ref{eq:widfact}) that greatly simplifies the
187: calculation.  The leading order partial widths are
188: \bea
189: \Gamma_{\mathrm LO}(\wprm\to t{\bar q}^\prime)&=&
190: \frac{g^2\beta^2}{16\pi m_{\wprm}} |V^\prime_{tq^\prime}|^2 (m^2_{\wprm}
191: + m^2_t/2)\,, \label{eq:wlot} \\
192: \Gamma_{\mathrm LO}(\wprm\to q{\bar q}^\prime)&=&\frac{g^2}{16\pi}
193: |V^\prime_{qq^\prime}|^2 m_{\wprm} \,, \label{eq:wloq} \\
194: \Gamma_{\mathrm LO}(\wprm\to l\bar\nu)&=&\frac{g^2}{16\pi}
195: |V^\prime_{l\nu}|^2 \frac{m_{\wprm}}{3} \,, \label{eq:wlol}
196: \eea
197: where $\beta=1-m^2_t/m^2_{\wprm}$, and we assume $g^2=8 m^2_W
198: G_F/\sqrt{2}$, as in the standard model.  Because we have assumed there
199: is at most one non-zero mass in the final state, the couplings appear
200: only in the combination
201: \beq
202: \bigl| g V^\prime_{f_if_j}\bigr|^2 \equiv 
203: \bigl| g_L \sin\zeta\, V^L_{f_if_j} \bigr|^2 + \bigl| g_R
204: \cos\zeta\, V^R_{f_if_j} \bigr|^2 \,. \label{eq:vprime}
205: \eeq
206: Hence, the partial widths of the \wpr boson have the same form as the
207: standard model $W$ boson, with the effect of new couplings and GCKM
208: matrix elements absorbed into $V^\prime_{f_if_j}$.
209: 
210: The above factorization of couplings turns out to hold in the
211: next-to-leading order widths as well.  The calculations of the
212: next-to-leading order partial widths of the $W$ boson were first
213: performed for the massless \cite{Albert:ix}, one mass
214: \cite{Alvarez:1987gi}, and arbitrary mass \cite{Lahanas:1996xx} final
215: states many years ago.  In order to derive the factorization of
216: arbitrary couplings above, however, we rederive the partial widths,
217: but use a newer calculational method whose results are needed in the
218: calculation of the fully differential cross section in
219: Sec.~\ref{sec:sigma}.
220: 
221: We evaluate the next-to-leading order partial widths to quarks by
222: using the phase-space-slicing method with two cutoffs
223: \cite{Harris:2001sx}.  In this method, phase space is divided into
224: three regions: soft (S), hard collinear (HC), and hard non-collinear
225: (H$\overline{\mathrm C}$).  The first two regions are integrated over
226: two-body phase space in $n=4-2\epsilon$ dimensions, whereas the third
227: region is integrated over three-body phase space in 4 dimensions with
228: cuts.
229: 
230: The soft region of phase space is defined in the \wpr rest frame by
231: a condition on the energy of the emitted gluon
232: \begin{equation}
233: \label{eq:appsg}
234:   E_g \leq \delta_s\, \frac{m_{\wprm}}{2} \,,
235: \end{equation}
236: where $\delta_s$ is an arbitrary parameter that must cancel in the
237: final result.  The hard region is the complement, $E_g > \delta_s\,
238: m_{\wprm}/2$. The gluon can only be collinear with a light quark, and
239: so the collinear region is defined by comparing the invariant mass
240: squared of the gluon and light quark to $\delta_c m^2_{\wprm}$, i.e.\
241: the collinear region is $s_{qg} = 2p_q\cdot p_g < \delta_c
242: m^2_{\wprm}$, where $p_{q,g}$ are quark and gluon four-momenta.  The
243: final result must be independent of $\delta_c$.  In practice we retain
244: terms logarithmic in $\delta_s$ or $\delta_c$, and drop terms that are
245: linear in the cutoffs.  At the end, we take the couplings numerically
246: to zero and show the solution contains no residual $\delta_s$ or
247: $\delta_c$ dependence.
248: 
249: The two-body next-to-leading order correction to the width is given by
250: \beq
251: \delta\Gamma_{2} = \frac{\alpha_s (m_{W^\prime})}{2\pi} C_F ( M^2_S + M^2_C
252: + M^2_V + \widetilde{M}^2_V ) \Gamma_{\mathrm LO} \,, \label{eq:wid2}
253: \eeq
254: where $C_F = 4/3$, and $\Gamma_{\mathrm LO}$ is listed in
255: Eqs.~(\ref{eq:wlot}, \ref{eq:wloq}).  If there is a top quark in the final
256: state, the terms are
257: \bea
258: M^2_S &=&2\ln^2(\delta_s) - 2\ln (\delta_s) \left[ 1 - \ln \left(
259: \frac{\mwpsq}{\mtsq} \right) \right] + \frac{\mwpsq + \mtsq}{\mwpsq -
260: \mtsq} \ln\! \left( \frac{\mwpsq}{\mtsq} \right) - 2 {\mathrm Li}_2(\beta)
261: - \frac{1}{2}\ln^2\! \left( \frac{\mwpsq}{\mtsq} \right) \,,
262: \label{eq:msf} \\
263: M^2_C &=& \frac{7}{2} - 2\zeta_2 - \ln^2(\delta_s) + 2 {\mathrm Li}_2\!
264: \left( \frac{\beta \delta_c}{\delta_s} \right) - \ln^2 (\beta) +2 \ln
265: (\delta_s) \ln (\beta) - \ln (\delta_c) \left( 2 \ln (\delta_s) +
266: \frac{3}{2} - 2 \ln (\beta) \right) \,, \label{eq:mcf} \\
267: M^2_V &=& -\frac{1}{2}\ln^2\! \left( \frac{\mwpsq}{\mtsq} \right) -
268: \frac{5}{2}\ln\! \left( \frac{\mwpsq}{\mtsq} \right) - \ln (1 - \lambda)
269: \left[ 2 + \beta + 2 \ln\! \left(
270: \frac{\mwpsq}{\mtsq} \right) \right] \nonumber \\
271: && - 6 - \ln^2 (1 - \lambda) + 2 {\mathrm Li}_2(\lambda) - 2\zeta_2 \,, 
272: \label{eq:mvf} \\
273: \widetilde{M}^2_V &=& \frac{\beta (1-\beta)}{2 (3-\beta)}\ln(1 - \lambda) \,,
274: \eea
275: where $\zeta_2 = \pi^2/6$, $\beta=1-m^2_t/m^2_{\wprm}$, and $\lambda =
276: 1/\beta$.  Note $(1 -\lambda) < 0$, which means $\ln (1 -\lambda) = \ln
277: |1 -\lambda|$, but $\ln^2 (1 -\lambda) = \ln^2 |1 -\lambda| - \pi^2$.
278: 
279: If both final-state quarks are massless, the formulae simplify to
280: \bea
281: M^2_S &=&4\ln^2(\delta_s) \,, \\
282: M^2_C &=& 7 - 4\zeta_2 - 2 \ln^2(\delta_s) + 4 {\mathrm Li}_2\! \left(
283: \frac{\delta_c}{\delta_s} \right) - \ln (\delta_c) [ 4 \ln (\delta_s)
284: + 3 ] \,, \\
285: M^2_V &=& - 8 + 4 \zeta_2 \,, \\
286: \widetilde{M}^2_V &=& 0 \,.
287: \eea
288: The sum of the terms in the massless case is
289: \beq
290: M^2 = 2\ln^2(\delta_s) - \ln
291: (\delta_c) [ 4 \ln (\delta_s) + 3 ] + 4 {\mathrm Li}_2\! \left(
292: \frac{\delta_c}{\delta_s} \right) - 1 \,. \label{eq:mmsq}
293: \eeq
294: 
295: \newcommand{\sttp}{s^\prime_{23}}
296: \newcommand{\sot}{s^{}_{13}}
297: \newcommand{\sotp}{s^\prime_{12}}
298: 
299: The three-body hard non-collinear real gluon emission term is evaluated
300: using a Monte Carlo integration in four dimensions, subject to the
301: cuts listed above.  The integrand is given by
302: \beq
303: d(\delta\Gamma_{3}) = \frac{1}{64\pi^3 m_{W^\prime}}
304: \overline{\Sigma}|M_3|^2 dE_g dE_{q^{\prime}} \; ,
305: \eeq
306: with
307: \beq
308: \overline{\Sigma}|M_3|^2 = -2\pi\alpha_s g^2 C_F
309: |V^{\prime}_{tq^\prime}|^2 \Psi_\Gamma \;,
310: \eeq
311: and
312: \bea
313: \Psi_\Gamma&=& 
314: 2\beta m_{\wprm}^2 (3-\beta)\biggl( \frac{\sotp}{\sot \sttp}
315: -\frac{m^2_t}{s^{\prime\,2}_{23}} \biggr) \nonumber \\
316: &&+ (3-\beta) \biggl(
317: \frac{\sot}{\sttp} + \frac{\sttp}{\sot} \biggr)
318: +2 (1-\beta) \;, \label{eq:appwid}
319: \eea
320: where $\beta=1-m^2_t/m^2_{\wprm}$, $\sotp = 2p_1\cdot p_2$, $\sot =
321: 2p_1\cdot p_3$, $\sttp = 2p_2\cdot p_3$, and $p_1$, $p_2$, and $p_3$
322: are the four-momenta of the light quark, top quark, and gluon,
323: respectively.  When both quarks are massless $\beta = 1$, and
324: Eq.~(\ref{eq:appwid}) is very simple.
325: 
326: Once we determine that the factorization of couplings holds for all
327: terms, the partial widths reduce to the expressions given in
328: Ref.~\cite{Alvarez:1987gi} with the replacement of CKM matrix elements
329: by the GCKM matrix elements $|V^\prime|^2$ defined in
330: Eq.~(\ref{eq:vprime}).  The massless case is simply
331: \beq
332: \Gamma_{\mathrm NLO}(\wprm\to q{\bar q}^\prime) = \biggl( 1 +
333: \frac{\alpha_s(m_{\wprm})}{\pi} \biggr) \Gamma_{\mathrm LO}(\wprm\to
334: q{\bar q}^\prime) \,.
335: \eeq
336: The massive case should reduce to Eq.~(12) of Ref.~\cite{Alvarez:1987gi},
337: \bea
338: \Gamma_{\mathrm NLO}(\wprm\to t{\bar q}^\prime) &=&
339: \Gamma_{\mathrm LO}(\wprm\to t{\bar q}^\prime) + \frac{g^2}{16\pi}
340: \frac{\alpha_s(m_{\wprm})}{4\pi} C_F |V^\prime_{tq^\prime}|^2 m_{\wprm}
341: \nonumber \\
342: &&\hspace*{8em} \times\{ \beta(1-\beta)(\beta-4) -
343: \beta^2(9-5\beta)\ln(\beta) - (1-\beta)
344: (4+6\beta-5\beta^2)\ln(1-\beta) 
345: \nonumber \\
346: &&\hspace*{9em} + \beta^2(3-\beta) [3/2 + 4 {\mathrm
347: Li }_2 (1-\beta) + 2 \ln(\beta)\ln(1-\beta) ] \} \,. \label{eq:alvwid}
348: \eea
349: 
350: 
351: \subsection{Numerical results}
352: \label{sec:numwid}
353: 
354: In order to be of immediate use to experimental analyses at the
355: Fermilab Tevatron, we make definite predictions of the \wpr partial
356: and total widths.  In all numerical results we use $m_t=175\pm 5$ GeV,
357: $G_F=1.16639\times 10^{-5}$ GeV$^{-2}$, and $m_W=80.4$ GeV.  We use a
358: two-loop running of $\alpha_s$ as defined in the CTEQ5M1 parton
359: distribution functions \cite{Lai:1999wy}.  We assume that
360: $V^\prime_{l\nu}$ is the identity matrix, and for
361: $V^\prime_{qq^\prime}$ we use the average Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa
362: (CKM) matrix \cite{Groom:in} with the exception that we assume
363: $|V^\prime_{tb}|=1$,
364: \beq
365: V^\prime_{\mathrm CKM} = \left(
366: \begin{array}{llc}
367: 0.9751 & 0.2215 & 0.0035 \\
368: 0.2210 & 0.9743 & 0.0410 \\
369: 0.0090 & 0.0400 & 1.0000
370: \end{array}
371: \right) \,. \label{eq:ckm}
372: \eeq
373: 
374: \begin{figure}[tbh]
375: \epsfxsize=3.375in
376: \centerline{\epsfbox{cwpss.ps}} 
377: \caption{Dependence of the NLO correction to the \wpr width on
378: $\delta_s = 300\times \delta_c$, for $m_{W^{\prime}}=500$ GeV.
379: $\delta\Gamma_{\mathrm NLO} = \delta\Gamma_2 + \delta\Gamma_3$, where
380: $\delta\Gamma_3$ refers to the H$\overline{\mathrm{C}}$ component, and
381: $\delta\Gamma_2$ to the sum of virtual, soft and hard-collinear
382: contributions.  The bottom region shows an enlargement of the
383: numerical prediction (circles) compared to the analytic prediction
384: (solid line) in Eq.~(\protect\ref{eq:alvwid}).\label{fig:wpss}}
385: \end{figure}
386: 
387: Before we discuss our results, we must show that our final result does
388: not depend on the cutoffs we choose.  To demonstrate this, we fix the
389: ratio of $\delta_s/\delta_c = 300$, and plot in Fig.~\ref{fig:wpss}
390: the NLO correction to the width of a \wpr of mass 500~GeV.  In the
391: upper half of the figure we see the logarithmic dependence in
392: $\delta_s$ and $\delta_c$ of the two- and three-body terms,
393: $\delta\Gamma_2$ and $\delta\Gamma_3$.  In the bottom half of the
394: figure we focus on the sum of the correction terms
395: $\delta\Gamma_{\mathrm NLO}$ for various values of $\delta_s$
396: (circles), and compare the result to the analytic prediction (solid
397: line) of Eq.~(\ref{eq:alvwid}).  Once $\delta_s \alt 10^{-3}$
398: ($\delta_c \alt 1/3\times 10^{-5}$), the result is stable to much less
399: than $1\%$ of the known NLO correction.

Accelerator Laboratory, Batavia, IL, 60510-0500}
