362:             _require_balanced(d, f"particle {self.class_name} definition")

374:     name: str  # LHS symbol

384: def _references(text: str, name: str) -> bool:
385:     """True if ``name`` appears in ``text`` as a whole Mathematica token."""
386:     if not text:
387:         return False
388:     return re.search(rf"(?<![A-Za-z0-9$]){re.escape(name)}(?![A-Za-z0-9$])", text) is not None
389: 
390: 
391: def _param_refs(p: Parameter, names: set) -> set:
392:     """Names of other parameters referenced by ``p``'s value/rules/definitions."""
393:     texts: List[str] = []
394:     if p.value:
395:         texts.append(p.value)
396:     for r in p.value_rules:
397:         texts.append(r.rhs)
398:     for r in p.definitions:
399:         texts.append(r.rhs)
400:     blob = " ".join(texts)
401:     return {n for n in names if n != p.name and _references(blob, n)}
402: 
403: 
404: def topo_sort_parameters(params: List[Parameter]) -> List[Parameter]:
405:     """Order parameters so each is defined before others that reference it.
406: 
407:     Stable (preserves input order among independent params). Raises on a
408:     dependency cycle.
409:     """
410:     names = {p.name for p in params}
411:     deps = {p.name: _param_refs(p, names) for p in params}
412:     by_name = {p.name: p for p in params}
413: 
414:     ordered: List[Parameter] = []
415:     emitted: set = set()
416:     remaining = [p.name for p in params]  # preserve input order
417: 
418:     while remaining:
419:         progressed = False
420:         still: List[str] = []
421:         for n in remaining:
422:             if deps[n] <= emitted:
423:                 ordered.append(by_name[n])
424:                 emitted.add(n)
425:                 progressed = True
426:             else:
427:                 still.append(n)
428:         remaining = still
429:         if not progressed:
430:             raise ValueError(
431:                 f"cyclic parameter dependency among: {sorted(remaining)}"
432:             )
433:     return ordered
434: 
435: 
436: _INDEX_SIZE = {"Generation": 3, "Colour": 3, "Gluon": 8, "SU2D": 2, "SU2W": 3}
437: 
438: 
439: def _block_entries(p: Parameter, sizes: Dict[str, int]) -> set:
440:     """The LHA entries (index tuples) an External parameter occupies in its block."""
441:     if not p.is_tensor:
442:         return {(p.order_block,)} if p.order_block is not None else set()
443:     entries = set()
444:     for r in p.value_rules:
445:         m = re.fullmatch(rf"\s*{re.escape(p.name)}\s*\[([0-9,\s]+)\]\s*", r.lhs)
446:         if m:
447:             entries.add(tuple(int(x) for x in m.group(1).split(",")))
448:     if entries:
449:         return entries
450:     ranges = [range(1, sizes.get(i, 3) + 1) for i in p.indices]
451:     out = {()}
452:     for rg in ranges:
453:         out = {e + (k,) for e in out for k in rg}
454:     return out
455: 
456: 
457: def _check_block_collisions(params: List[Parameter], sizes: Dict[str, int]) -> None:
458:     """External parameters that share an LHA block must not share an entry.
459: 
460:     FeynRules files an External tensor's entries under (block, i, j) and a
461:     scalar under (block, OrderBlock). Two parameters on one entry leave the UFO
462:     with one name defined twice, and MadGraph rejects the model ("name VLq1x1
463:     define multiple time"). Tensors of different rank in one block do not
464:     collide: GeneralU1's yN[i] and ynu[i,j] share a block and import cleanly.
465:     """
466:     by_block: Dict[str, List[Parameter]] = {}
467:     for p in params:
468:         if p.parameter_type == ParamType.External and p.block_name:
469:             by_block.setdefault(p.block_name, []).append(p)
470:     for block, ps in by_block.items():
471:         owner: Dict[tuple, str] = {}
472:         for p in ps:
473:             for e in sorted(_block_entries(p, sizes)):
474:                 if e in owner and owner[e] != p.name:
475:                     raise ValueError(
476:                         f"External parameters {owner[e]} and {p.name} both occupy "
477:                         f"block {block!r} entry {list(e)}: the UFO would define one "
478:                         "name twice. Give one of them its own block_name (or, for "
479:                         "scalars, its own order_block)"
480:                     )
481:                 owner[e] = p.name
482:

502:     raw_blocks: List[str] = []  # emitted just before Lagrangian terms

Contract a doublet with an anti-doublet on a shared index: `LLbar[sp, ii, ff] ... Phi[ii]`. Contract two objects of the same conjugation type (`LLbar` with `Phibar`, `QLbar` with `Phibar`, i.e. any term the paper writes with `Htilde = i tau2 H*`) with `Eps[ii, jj]` on two distinct indices: `LLbar[sp, ii, ff] ... Phibar[jj] Eps[ii, jj]`. Never contract `LLbar[ii]` with `Phibar[ii]`. Model the SM Yukawas: `QLbar.dR Phi[ii]`, `LLbar.lR Phi[ii]`, `QLbar.uR Phibar[jj] Eps[ii, jj]`.

Do not copy a paper's charge table literally when the paper's Yukawa equation and its table use different hypercharge conventions (for example the paper effectively uses Y(H) = -1/2). Re-derive the new-U(1) charge of every SM field, including the Higgs, from the requirement that all SM Yukawas and all new Yukawas are invariant under SM.fr conventions. Report which sign you chose and why. Do not put quantum numbers on a `SelfConjugate -> True` class; put a chiral charge on an Unphysical chiral class instead.

6. Read only the paper. Do not open any cached or reference `.fr` file for the same model. If you see one, say so in the output and do not use it.

7. Fractions and roots in extracted equations. The paper text is machine-extracted. A displayed fraction or radical can arrive flattened: the numerator, the fraction bar and the denominator become separate lines, so `A / Sqrt[B]` and `A Sqrt[B]` look identical. For every coefficient that contains a fraction, a square root or a power:
   - If a LaTeX source file (`*_source.tex`) is available, read the `\frac{...}{...}` and `\sqrt{...}` there and take it literally. The LaTeX is authoritative over the flattened text.

Class names, parameter names and index names must not be Mathematica built-ins or FeynRules symbols: never `N`, `C`, `D`, `E`, `I`, `K`, `O`, `HC`, `CC`, `FS`, `DC`, `del`, `Eps`, `Ga`, `ProjP`, `ProjM`, and never a name SM.fr already declares (`H`, `Phi`, `Z`, `W`, `A`, `G`, `ee`, `gs`, `gw`, `sw`, `cw`, `vev`, `MZ`, `MW`, ...). 710:   feynmangaugerules = If[Not[FeynmanGauge], {G0|GP|GPbar ->0}, {}];
711:  
712:   yuk = ExpandIndices[
713:    -yd[ff2, ff3] CKM[ff1, ff2] QLbar[sp, ii, ff1, cc].dR [sp, ff3, cc] Phi[ii] - 
714:     yl[ff1, ff3] LLbar[sp, ii, ff1].lR [sp, ff3] Phi[ii] - 
715:     yu[ff1, ff2] QLbar[sp, ii, ff1, cc].uR [sp, ff2, cc] Phibar[jj] Eps[ii, jj], FlavorExpand -> SU2D];

717:   yuk+HC[yuk]/.feynmangaugerules
718:  ];

720: LGhost := Block[{LGh1,LGhw,LGhs,LGhphi,mu, generators,gh,ghbar,Vectorize,phi1,phi2,togoldstones,doublet,doublet0},
721:   (* Pure gauge piece *) 	
722:   LGh1 = -ghBbar.del[DC[ghB,mu],mu];
723:   LGhw = -ghWibar[ii].del[DC[ghWi[ii],mu],mu];
724:   LGhs = -ghGbar[ii].del[DC[ghG[ii],mu],mu];
725: 
726:   (* Scalar pieces: see Peskin pages 739-742 *)
727:   (* phi1 and phi2 are the real degrees of freedom of GP *)
728:   (* Vectorize transforms a doublet in a vector in the phi-basis, i.e. the basis of real degrees of freedom *)
729:   gh    = {ghB, ghWi[1], ghWi[2], ghWi[3]};
730:   ghbar = {ghBbar, ghWibar[1], ghWibar[2], ghWibar[3]};
731:   generators = {-I/2 g1 IdentityMatrix[2], -I/2 gw PauliSigma[1], -I/2 gw PauliSigma[2], -I/2 gw PauliSigma[3]};
732:   doublet = Expand[{(-I phi1 - phi2)/Sqrt[2], Phi[2]} /. MR$Definitions /. vev -> 0]; 
733:   doublet0 = {0, vev/Sqrt[2]};
734:   Vectorize[{a_, b_}]:= Simplify[{Sqrt[2] Re[Expand[a]], Sqrt[2] Im[Expand[a]], Sqrt[2] Re[Expand[b]], Sqrt[2] Im[Expand[b]]}/.{Im[_]->0, Re[num_]->num}];
735:   togoldstones := {phi1 -> (GP + GPbar)/Sqrt[2], phi2 -> (-GP + GPbar)/(I Sqrt[2])};
736:   LGhphi=Plus@@Flatten[Table[-ghbar[[kkk]].gh[[lll]] Vectorize[generators[[kkk]].doublet0].Vectorize[generators[[lll]].(doublet+doublet0)],{kkk,4},{lll,4}]] /.togoldstones;
737: 
738: ExpandIndices[ LGhs + If[FeynmanGauge, LGh1 + LGhw + LGhphi,0], FlavorExpand->SU2W]];
739: 
740: LSM:= LGauge + LFermions + LHiggs + LYukawa + LGhost;

30: We present the fully differential production and decay of a $W^\prime$
31: boson, with arbitrary vector and axial-vector couplings, to any final
32: state at next-to-leading order in QCD.  We demonstrate a complete
33: factorization of couplings at next-to-leading order in both the
34: partial width of the $W^\prime$ boson, and in the full two-to-two
35: cross section.  We provide numerical predictions for the contribution
36: of a $W^\prime$ boson to single-top-quark production, and separate
37: results based on whether the mass of the right-handed neutrino $\nu_R$
38: is light enough for the leptonic decay channel to be open.  The
39: single-top-quark analysis will allow for an improved direct $W^\prime$
40: mass limit of 525--550~GeV using data from run I of the Fermilab
41: Tevatron.  We propose a modified tolerance method for estimating
42: parton distribution function uncertainties in cross sections.
43: \end{abstract}
44: 
45: \section{Introduction}
46: 
47: Since the introduction of the standard model, many extensions have
48: been proposed that involve enhanced gauge symmetries.  One common
49: feature of these models is the prediction of additional gauge bosons,
50: generically called \wpr and $Z^\prime$ bosons.  In non-universal and
51: top-flavor models, the \wpr gauge boson arises from a new SU(2)$_L$
52: sector that distinguishes between generations of fermions
53: \cite{Li:nk,Malkawi:1996fs,Muller:1996dj}, and may treat quarks and
54: leptons differently \cite{Georgi:1989ic,Georgi:1989xz,He:1999vp}.  The
55: \wpr boson could be the lowest Kaluza-Klein mode of the $W$ boson
56: \cite{Datta:2000gm}, or a heavy mass eigenstate in non-commuting
57: extended technicolor \cite{Chivukula:1995gu}.  In a left-right
58: symmetric model the \wpr and standard-model $W$ bosons are remnants of
59: a broken ${\mathrm SU(2)}_L \times {\mathrm SU(2)}_R$ symmetry
60: \cite{Pati:1974yy,Mohapatra:1974hk,Mohapatra:1974gc,Senjanovic:1975rk}.
61: The resulting left-right mixing may be naturally suppressed by
62: orbifold breaking of the left-right symmetry \cite{Mimura:2002te}, or
63: by supersymmetric interactions \cite{Cvetic:1983su}.  While indirect
64: bounds may be placed on the masses and couplings of these various \wpr
65: bosons within the context of their explicit theories, it is always
66: advantageous to search for these new particles directly.  In order to
67: facilitate a direct experimental search, and to achieve the most
68: general contact with theory, we calculate the fully differential
69: next-to-leading order cross section for the production and decay of a
70: \wpr boson to any final state with arbitrary vector and axial-vector
71: couplings.
72: 
73: The most general Lorentz invariant Lagrangian describing the coupling
74: of a \wpr to fermions may be written as
75: \beq
76: {\cal L} = \frac{g}{\sqrt{2}} \overline{f}_i\gamma_\mu \bigl(
77: C^R_{f_if_j} P_R + C^L_{f_if_j} P_L \bigr) W^{\prime} f_j +
78: \mathrm{H.c.} \,, \label{eq:genlan}
79: \eeq
80: where $P_{R,L}=(1\pm \gamma_5)/2$, $g$ is the standard model SU(2)$_L$
81: coupling, and the $C^{R,L}_{f_if_j}$ are arbitrary couplings that
82: differ for quarks and leptons.  For a standard model $W$ boson,
83: $C^R=0$, and $C^L$ is either the Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa matrix or
84: diagonal, for quarks or leptons, respectively.
85: 
86: Most experimental searches have concentrated on \wpr bosons that decay
87: via a purely left- or right-handed current.  In order to make contact
88: with these results, we rewrite Eq.~(\ref{eq:genlan}) in the notation
89: typical of left-right symmetric models as \cite{Langacker:1989xa}
90: \beq
91: {\cal L} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \overline{f}_i\gamma_\mu \bigl( g_R
92: e^{i\omega} \cos\zeta\, V^R_{f_if_j} P_R + g_L \sin\zeta\, V^L_{f_if_j}
93: P_L\bigr) W^{\prime} f_j + \mathrm{H.c.} \,, \label{eq:lagrangian}
94: \eeq
95: where $\zeta$ is a left-right mixing angle, and $\omega$ is a
96: CP-violating phase that can be absorbed into $V^R$.  In this notation,
97: $g_{R(L)}$ are the right (left) gauge couplings, and
98: $V^{R,L}_{f_if_j}$ are generalized Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa (GCKM)
99: matrices.  In models where the $W$ and \wpr mix, the mixing angle
100: $\zeta$ is usually constrained to be small ($|\zeta|<$ a few $\times
101: 10^{-5}$--$10^{-2}$ \cite{Groom:in}).  Hence, the search for purely
102: right- or left-handed states appears well motivated.
103: 
104: Many direct searches for \wpr bosons have been performed at hadron
105: colliders.  Most experimental analyses have considered left- or
106: right-handed \wpr bosons, with standard-model-like couplings, that
107: decay into leptonic final states.  Left-handed $W^\prime_L$ bosons, or
108: right-handed $W^\prime_R$ bosons in which the decay into a
109: right-handed neutrino $\nu_R$ is kinematically allowed, are
110: constrained to have masses $m_{\wprm} > 786$~GeV
111: \cite{Arnison:1983zy,Arnison:ut,Ansari:1987ch,Albajar:1988ka,Abe:1994zg,Abachi:1995yi,Abe:1999gz,Affolder:2001gr}.
112: If $m_{\nu_R} \agt m_{\wprm}$ the decay to $\nu_R$ is not allowed,
113: and the right-handed $W^\prime_R$ bosons are only directly constrained
114: by peak searches in the dijet data.  Unless the \wpr has greatly
115: enhanced couplings to light quarks, the dijet data are limited by QCD
116: backgrounds to providing a mass limit of $420$~GeV
117: \cite{Alitti:1990kw,Alitti:1993pn,Abe:1997hm}.
118: 
119: The only final state not measured by one of the experiments listed
120: above involves the decay of a \wpr to a single top quark.  In
121: Refs.~\cite{Simmons:1996ws,Tait:1997fe} it was pointed out that a
122: deviation of measured the single-top-quark cross section from the
123: standard model prediction could be evidence of a new gauge
124: interaction.  In the context of models with \wpr bosons, we wish to
125: take this one step further, and propose that the experiments search
126: for an explicit \wpr mass peak in the $s$-channel single-top-quark
127: sample.  We examine just how large the cross section into single top
128: quarks can be at the Fermilab Tevatron and Large Hadron Collider (LHC)
129: as a function of \wpr mass, and determine how enhanced or suppressed
130: couplings enter into the measurable cross section after cuts.  We also
131: determine the next-to-leading order distributions of the final-state
132: jets to estimate the effect on the reconstruction of the \wpr mass
133: peak.
134: 
135: A \wpr boson that propagates in the $s$-channel appears very similar
136: to Drell-Yan production.  We might be tempted to use the
137: next-to-next-to-leading order (NNLO) predictions for Drell-Yan
138: \cite{Hamberg:1990np} (or the updates in
139: Ref.~\cite{Harlander:2002wh}).  However, these calculations are not
140: adequate to predict the cross section for \wpr bosons which decay to
141: quarks.  There are two reasons for this.  The first problem is that
142: the final state effects are very large.  Not only are there large QCD
143: corrections to the quark final state, but the top-quark mass has a
144: large effect on the branching fraction when it is in the final state.
145: The second reason is that there are initial- and final-state
146: interference terms that arise at NNLO that are of an unknown size.
147: (Pure QCD processes also interfere at NNLO, e.g.\ with $u\bar d \to
148: u\bar d$ via the exchange of two gluons.)  Therefore, we cannot simply
149: take the NNLO production as calculated and append a Breit-Wigner
150: propagator that uses leading or next-to-leading order widths.
151: Instead, we perform the complete calculation at next-to-leading order.
152: 
153: We organize the paper as follows.  In Sec.~\ref{sec:width} we
154: calculate the partial widths into leptons or quarks, including the
155: effects of the top-quark mass, for the \wpr boson using arbitrary
156: vector and axial-vector couplings at next-to-leading order (NLO) in
157: QCD.  We demonstrate that the couplings factorize, and present some
158: numerical results for partial widths and branching fractions into a
159: top-quark final state.  In Sec.~\ref{sec:sigma} we calculate the fully
160: differential production and decay of a \wpr into any final state at
161: NLO in QCD.  We present numerical results for the single-top-quark
162: production cross section via $s$-channel exchange of a \wpr boson.  We
163: asses all theoretical uncertainties, and propose a modification of the
164: tolerance method for calculating parton distribution function
165: uncertainties.  Finally, we present the NLO jet distributions, discuss
166: the effect of jet definitions on these distributions, and estimate the
167: limits that may be placed on the \wpr mass using data from run I and
168: run II of the Fermilab Tevatron.
169: 
170: \section{Next-to-leading order width}
171: \label{sec:width}
172: 
173: We divide our evaluation of the \wpr width into three terms that
174: depend on the final decay products:
175: \beq
176: \Gamma_{\mathrm tot}(\wprm) = \Gamma (\wprm\to t{\bar q}^\prime)
177: +\Gamma (\wprm\to q{\bar q}^\prime) + \Gamma (\wprm\to l\bar\nu) \,.
178: \label{eq:widfact}
179: \eeq
180: We separate the partial widths containing a top quark from those
181: containing only massless quarks so that we may retain an explicit
182: top-quark mass dependence in the width.
183: 
184: While the large number of couplings in Eq.~(\ref{eq:lagrangian})
185: appears daunting, a factorization of the couplings occurs in the
186: partial widths of Eq.~(\ref{eq:widfact}) that greatly simplifies the
187: calculation.  The leading order partial widths are
188: \bea
189: \Gamma_{\mathrm LO}(\wprm\to t{\bar q}^\prime)&=&
190: \frac{g^2\beta^2}{16\pi m_{\wprm}} |V^\prime_{tq^\prime}|^2 (m^2_{\wprm}
191: + m^2_t/2)\,, \label{eq:wlot} \\
192: \Gamma_{\mathrm LO}(\wprm\to q{\bar q}^\prime)&=&\frac{g^2}{16\pi}
193: |V^\prime_{qq^\prime}|^2 m_{\wprm} \,, \label{eq:wloq} \\
194: \Gamma_{\mathrm LO}(\wprm\to l\bar\nu)&=&\frac{g^2}{16\pi}
195: |V^\prime_{l\nu}|^2 \frac{m_{\wprm}}{3} \,, \label{eq:wlol}
196: \eea
197: where $\beta=1-m^2_t/m^2_{\wprm}$, and we assume $g^2=8 m^2_W
198: G_F/\sqrt{2}$, as in the standard model.  Because we have assumed there
199: is at most one non-zero mass in the final state, the couplings appear
200: only in the combination
201: \beq
202: \bigl| g V^\prime_{f_if_j}\bigr|^2 \equiv 
203: \bigl| g_L \sin\zeta\, V^L_{f_if_j} \bigr|^2 + \bigl| g_R
204: \cos\zeta\, V^R_{f_if_j} \bigr|^2 \,. \label{eq:vprime}
205: \eeq
206: Hence, the partial widths of the \wpr boson have the same form as the
207: standard model $W$ boson, with the effect of new couplings and GCKM
208: matrix elements absorbed into $V^\prime_{f_if_j}$.
209: 
210: The above factorization of couplings turns out to hold in the
211: next-to-leading order widths as well.  The calculations of the
212: next-to-leading order partial widths of the $W$ boson were first
213: performed for the massless \cite{Albert:ix}, one mass
214: \cite{Alvarez:1987gi}, and arbitrary mass \cite{Lahanas:1996xx} final
215: states many years ago.  In order to derive the factorization of
216: arbitrary couplings above, however, we rederive the partial widths,
217: but use a newer calculational method whose results are needed in the
218: calculation of the fully differential cross section in
219: Sec.~\ref{sec:sigma}.
220: 
221: We evaluate the next-to-leading order partial widths to quarks by
222: using the phase-space-slicing method with two cutoffs
223: \cite{Harris:2001sx}.  In this method, phase space is divided into
224: three regions: soft (S), hard collinear (HC), and hard non-collinear
225: (H$\overline{\mathrm C}$).  The first two regions are integrated over
226: two-body phase space in $n=4-2\epsilon$ dimensions, whereas the third
227: region is integrated over three-body phase space in 4 dimensions with
228: cuts.
229: 
230: The soft region of phase space is defined in the \wpr rest frame by
231: a condition on the energy of the emitted gluon
232: \begin{equation}
233: \label{eq:appsg}
234:   E_g \leq \delta_s\, \frac{m_{\wprm}}{2} \,,
235: \end{equation}
236: where $\delta_s$ is an arbitrary parameter that must cancel in the
237: final result.  The hard region is the complement, $E_g > \delta_s\,
238: m_{\wprm}/2$. The gluon can only be collinear with a light quark, and
239: so the collinear region is defined by comparing the invariant mass
240: squared of the gluon and light quark to $\delta_c m^2_{\wprm}$, i.e.\
241: the collinear region is $s_{qg} = 2p_q\cdot p_g < \delta_c
242: m^2_{\wprm}$, where $p_{q,g}$ are quark and gluon four-momenta.  The
243: final result must be independent of $\delta_c$.  In practice we retain
244: terms logarithmic in $\delta_s$ or $\delta_c$, and drop terms that are
245: linear in the cutoffs.  At the end, we take the couplings numerically
246: to zero and show the solution contains no residual $\delta_s$ or
247: $\delta_c$ dependence.

matrices.  In models where the $W$ and \wpr mix, the mixing angle
$\zeta$ is usually constrained to be small ($|\zeta|<$ a few $\times
10^{-5}$--$10^{-2}$ \cite{Groom:in}).  Hence, the search for purely
right- or left-handed states appears well motivated.

Many direct searches for \wpr bosons have been performed at hadron
colliders.  Most experimental analyses have considered left- or
right-handed \wpr bosons, with standard-model-like couplings, that
decay into leptonic final states.  Left-handed $W^\prime_L$ bosons, or
right-handed $W^\prime_R$ bosons in which the decay into a
right-handed neutrino $\nu_R$ is kinematically allowed, are
constrained to have masses $m_{\wprm} > 786$~GeV
\cite{Arnison:1983zy,Arnison:ut,Ansari:1987ch,Albajar:1988ka,Abe:1994zg,Abachi:1995yi,Abe:1999gz,Affolder:2001gr}.
If $m_{\nu_R} \agt m_{\wprm}$ the decay to $\nu_R$ is not allowed,
and the right-handed $W^\prime_R$ bosons are only directly constrained
by peak searches in the dijet data.  Unless the \wpr has greatly
enhanced couplings to light quarks, the dijet data are limited by QCD
backgrounds to providing a mass limit of $420$~GeV
\cite{Alitti:1990kw,Alitti:1993pn,Abe:1997hm}.

The only final state not measured by one of the experiments listed
above involves the decay of a \wpr to a single top quark.  In
Refs.~\cite{Simmons:1996ws,Tait:1997fe} it was pointed out that a
deviation of measured the single-top-quark cross section from the
standard model prediction could be evidence of a new gauge
interaction.  In the context of models with \wpr bosons, we wish to
take this one step further, and propose that the experiments search
for an explicit \wpr mass peak in the $s$-channel single-top-quark
sample.  We examine just how large the cross section into single top
quarks can be at the Fermilab Tevatron and Large Hadron Collider (LHC)
as a function of \wpr mass, and determine how enhanced or suppressed
couplings enter into the measurable cross section after cuts.  We also
determine the next-to-leading order distributions of the final-state
jets to estimate the effect on the reconstruction of the \wpr mass
peak.

A \wpr boson that propagates in the $s$-channel appears very similar
to Drell-Yan production.  We might be tempted to use the
next-to-next-to-leading order (NNLO) predictions for Drell-Yan
\cite{Hamberg:1990np} (or the updates in
Ref.~\cite{Harlander:2002wh}).  However, these calculations are not
adequate to predict the cross section for \wpr bosons which decay to
quarks.  There are two reasons for this.  The first problem is that
the final state effects are very large.  Not only are there large QCD
corrections to the quark final state, but the top-quark mass has a
large effect on the branching fraction when it is in the final state.
The second reason is that there are initial- and final-state
interference terms that arise at NNLO that are of an unknown size.
(Pure QCD processes also interfere at NNLO, e.g.\ with $u\bar d \to
u\bar d$ via the exchange of two gluons.)  Therefore, we cannot simply
take the NNLO production as calculated and append a Breit-Wigner
propagator that uses leading or next-to-leading order widths.
Instead, we perform the complete calculation at next-to-leading order.

We organize the paper as follows.  In Sec.~\ref{sec:width} we
calculate the partial widths into leptons or quarks, including the
effects of the top-quark mass, for the \wpr boson using arbitrary
vector and axial-vector couplings at next-to-leading order (NLO) in
QCD.  We demonstrate that the couplings factorize, and present some
numerical results for partial widths and branching fractions into a
top-quark final state.  In Sec.~\ref{sec:sigma} we calculate the fully
differential production and decay of a \wpr into any final state at
NLO in QCD.  We present numerical results for the single-top-quark
production cross section via $s$-channel exchange of a \wpr boson.  We
asses all theoretical uncertainties, and propose a modification of the
tolerance method for calculating parton distribution function
uncertainties.  Finally, we present the NLO jet distributions, discuss
the effect of jet definitions on these distributions, and estimate the
limits that may be placed on the \wpr mass using data from run I and
run II of the Fermilab Tevatron.

\section{Next-to-leading order width}
\label{sec:width}

We divide our evaluation of the \wpr width into three terms that
depend on the final decay products:
\beq
\Gamma_{\mathrm tot}(\wprm) = \Gamma (\wprm\to t{\bar q}^\prime)
+\Gamma (\wprm\to q{\bar q}^\prime) + \Gamma (\wprm\to l\bar\nu) \,.
\label{eq:widfact}
\eeq
We separate the partial widths containing a top quark from those
containing only massless quarks so that we may retain an explicit
top-quark mass dependence in the width.

While the large number of couplings in Eq.~(\ref{eq:lagrangian})
appears daunting, a factorization of the couplings occurs in the
partial widths of Eq.~(\ref{eq:widfact}) that greatly simplifies the
calculation.  The leading order partial widths are
\bea
\Gamma_{\mathrm LO}(\wprm\to t{\bar q}^\prime)&=&
\frac{g^2\beta^2}{16\pi m_{\wprm}} |V^\prime_{tq^\prime}|^2 (m^2_{\wprm}
+ m^2_t/2)\,, \label{eq:wlot} \\
\Gamma_{\mathrm LO}(\wprm\to q{\bar q}^\prime)&=&\frac{g^2}{16\pi}
|V^\prime_{qq^\prime}|^2 m_{\wprm} \,, \label{eq:wloq} \\
\Gamma_{\mathrm LO}(\wprm\to l\bar\nu)&=&\frac{g^2}{16\pi}
|V^\prime_{l\nu}|^2 \frac{m_{\wprm}}{3} \,, \label{eq:wlol}
\eea
where $\beta=1-m^2_t/m^2_{\wprm}$, and we assume $g^2=8 m^2_W
G_F/\sqrt{2}$, as in the standard model.  Because we have assumed there
is at most one non-zero mass in the final state, the couplings appear
only in the combination
\beq
\bigl| g V^\prime_{f_if_j}\bigr|^2 \equiv 
\bigl| g_L \sin\zeta\, V^L_{f_if_j} \bigr|^2 + \bigl| g_R
\cos\zeta\, V^R_{f_if_j} \bigr|^2 \,. \label{eq:vprime}
\eeq
Hence, the partial widths of the \wpr boson have the same form as the
standard model $W$ boson, with the effect of new couplings and GCKM
matrix elements absorbed into $V^\prime_{f_if_j}$.

The above factorization of couplings turns out to hold in the
next-to-leading order widths as well.  The calculations of the
next-to-leading order partial widths of the $W$ boson were first
performed for the massless \cite{Albert:ix}, one mass
\cite{Alvarez:1987gi}, and arbitrary mass \cite{Lahanas:1996xx} final
states many years ago.  In order to derive the factorization of
arbitrary couplings above, however, we rederive the partial widths,
but use a newer calculational method whose results are needed in the
calculation of the fully differential cross section in
Sec.~\ref{sec:sigma}.

We evaluate the next-to-leading order partial widths to quarks by
using the phase-space-slicing method with two cutoffs
\cite{Harris:2001sx}.  In this method, phase space is divided into
three regions: soft (S), hard collinear (HC), and hard non-collinear
(H$\overline{\mathrm C}$).  The first two regions are integrated over
two-body phase space in $n=4-2\epsilon$ dimensions, whereas the third
region is integrated over three-body phase space in 4 dimensions with
cuts.

The soft region of phase space is defined in the \wpr rest frame by
a condition on the energy of the emitted gluon
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:appsg}
  E_g \leq \delta_s\, \frac{m_{\wprm}}{2} \,,
\end{equation}
where $\delta_s$ is an arbitrary parameter that must cancel in the
final result.  The hard region is the complement, $E_g > \delta_s\,
m_{\wprm}/2$. The gluon can only be collinear with a light quark, and
so the collinear region is defined by comparing the invariant mass
squared of the gluon and light quark to $\delta_c m^2_{\wprm}$, i.e.\
the collinear region is $s_{qg} = 2p_q\cdot p_g < \delta_c
m^2_{\wprm}$, where $p_{q,g}$ are quark and gluon four-momenta.  The
final result must be independent of $\delta_c$.  In practice we retain
terms logarithmic in $\delta_s$ or $\delta_c$, and drop terms that are
linear in the cutoffs.  At the end, we take the couplings numerically
to zero and show the solution contains no residual $\delta_s$ or
$\delta_c$ dependence.

36: def _bool(b: bool) -> str:

40: def _quote(s: str) -> str:

46:     if len(items) == 1:

48:     return "{" + ", ".join(_quote(x) for x in items) + "}"

52:     """ParticleName/FullName/PropagatorLabel: str -> quoted; list -> {...}."""
53:     if isinstance(v, list):
54:         return "{" + ", ".join(_quote(x) for x in v) + "}"

69: # etc. are REPRESENTATION labels fixed by a field's Indices, not quantum numbers;
70: # if left in QuantumNumbers, FeynRules emits an unevaluated `Colour[field]` into
71: # the UFO's particles.py, which MadGraph rejects with "name 'Colour' is not
72: # defined". Drop these reserved index/representation names.
73: _REP_LABELS = {
74:     "Colour", "Color", "Sextet", "Gluon", "Generation", "Spin", "Lorentz",
75:     "SU2", "SU2W", "SU2L", "SU2D", "SU2R",

83: def _reserved_mass_width_names(particles) -> set:

85:     specs. Declaring them again in M$Parameters double-defines the name in the UFO
86:     (MadGraph InvalidModel), so the renderer drops those duplicates."""
87:     names: set = set()
88:     for p in particles or []:
89:         for spec in (getattr(p, "mass", None), getattr(p, "width", None)):
90:             if spec is None:
91:                 continue
92:             if getattr(spec, "sym", None):
93:                 names.add(spec.sym)
94:             for sub, _val in (getattr(spec, "members", None) or []):
95:                 names.add(sub)

99: def _is_internal_param(p) -> bool:
100:     """Internal/derived parameters carry a formula (Definitions) that FeynRules
101:     cannot auto-create from a particle Mass/Width spec, so they must stay in
102:     M$Parameters even when named like a mass/width (e.g. a computed decay width
103:     Width -> {WV1, Internal}). Only plain External duplicates are dropped."""
104:     if getattr(p, "definitions", None):

113: def _interaction_order(t: Tuple[str, int]) -> str:

117: def _mw_value(v):
118:     """Normalize a mass/width value. FeynRules' ``Automatic`` width is computed
119:     only when AddDecays is on — which is off for us (broken on Wolfram >=15), so
120:     it leaks the literal ``Automatic`` into the UFO and MadGraph fails with
121:     ``name 'Automatic' is not defined``. Emit a numeric placeholder instead;
122:     MadGraph's compute_widths recovers the real width from the model."""
123:     return "1." if str(v).strip().lower() == "automatic" else v

126: def _mass(m: MassSpec) -> str:
127:     if m.massless:
128:         return "0"

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Deterministic lints for an agent-written FeynRules add-on (.fr) file.

Every rule encodes one construct that broke a compile, a FeynRules check or a
MadGraph import in the benchmark (prompt_addendum_v3.txt rules 9-15 and the
repair-loop taxonomy). A lint runs in milliseconds on the text; the compile it
predicts takes up to 900 s.

Each finding carries the STAGE it predicts:
  compile  - FeynRules will not load or will not finish the model
  checks   - the model loads but a consistency check fails
  mg5      - the UFO is written but MadGraph rejects it
  harness  - the validation harness cannot pick the total Lagrangian
  warn     - FeynRules warns; the run may still pass

Library: ``lint_text(text) -> list[Finding]``. CLI: ``fr_lint.py file.fr``.
"""

from __future__ import annotations
